en: The Great Ocean of Āyurveda.
The method of food and drink... [is such that] the harītakī fruit is like a mother to men, producing the purification of urine, feces, and other impurities. // 5 //

In summer, one should administer it with an equal amount of jaggery and rock salt; at the onset of the rainy season, with an equal amount of sugar; and in autumn, with an equal amount of ginger (*amalaya*); and at the arrival of the winter cold, one should employ it [with appropriate adjuncts].
O King, in the cool season or during the springtime, consume long pepper combined with honey, like a myrobalan fruit; may your enemies perish like your diseases. // 6 //
Those who delight in lack of exertion during the springtime, who are fond of sexual intercourse in summer,

who are attached to the water of puddles in the rainy season and loathe the water of new wells, who take pleasure in pungent, sour, and hot foods in autumn, who eat curd in the early winter, and who are sluggish with sleep in the deep winter— [these are the characteristics of those born under the asterism Mūla].
But for you who plunge into cold water during the winter, may your enemies perish! (7)
Now, the section on water:
The enchanting water of the Gaṅgā is sweet in taste and post-digestive effect, cooling, pacifies the three doṣas, is purifying, highly wholesome, and delightful. (8)

The water of the Bhagirathi is declared to be sweet, clear, and exceedingly pleasing; it is wholesome, digestible, and a purifier that removes sin. It destroys thirst and delusion, is supremely pure, and bestows wisdom. (9)
Thus ends the section on *gāṅga*.
Therefore, there is nothing more weighty, more delicious, or more supreme for removing *pitta* than this.
The water of the Yamunā is wind-increasing, fire-generating, and dry.
Thus [described is] the water from the Yamunā.
The water of the Narmadā is extremely clear, excellent, cooling, light, and scraping;
it pacifies pitta and kapha and conquers all diseases. (11)
Thus, water originating from the Godāvarī is supreme for alleviating itching and skin diseases (kaṇḍū-kuṣṭha), stimulating the digestive fire,
acting as a digestive aid, and subduing wind and bile.

The water of the Godāvarī removes afflictions of bile, blood, and wind; it cures skin diseases and other ailments caused by corrupted humors; it is supremely wholesome, a digestive stimulant, a destroyer of sins, and a quencher of thirst. (13)
Thus [is the description] of the Godāvarī. The water of the Kṛṣṇaveṇī is somewhat lighter and sweet, yet it is rough, cold, and aggravates vāta and rakta. (14)
Thus [ends the section] on the Kṛṣṇaveṇī.
The water of the Kāverī is wholesome, destroys undigested matter (āma), bestows strength and complexion, is fiery in nature yet extremely cooling, and removes ringworm, leprosy, and poisons. (15)

Thus [is described] the water of the Kāverī: it pacifies the three humors (doṣas), is wholesome, delicious, heart-pleasing, and life-sustaining; it destroys dizziness, quenches thirst, and is divine, enchanting water. (16)
Thus ends [the section on] Akālajalada. The minor rivers born from the intermediate directions remove the three doshas; the great rivers flowing southward destroy pitta and kapha.
Rivers originating in the northern direction are wholesome, light, and remove the three doshas;
those arising in the eastern region immediately dispel wind and phlegm.
The western [medicinal plants] cause the discharge of bile and destroy phlegm and wind. // 17 //
Thus, the rivers and minor streams have now been described in brief.
Sea water is foul-smelling, saline, and causes all the bodily humors to become deranged. (18)
It is harmful to the eyes, yet it destroys intoxication, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, and upward movement of wind (udāvarta).
Now, regarding the characteristics of the eight types of water: I shall explain the qualities and defects of celestial water and the others through careful consideration. (19)
Celestial, atmospheric, river-born, well-water, water from a spring, lake-born, tank-born, and mountain-born—water is traditionally said to be of eight kinds. (20)
Water that resembles great beryl released from autumn clouds, which removes all defects and is sweet, is called divine. 21.
Water released from the clouds of the rainy season, characterized by an indistinct sweetness and resembling crystal, is known as *āntarikṣa*.
Water originating from a river that flows from a mountain, possessing the luster of a *gomedaka* gem, and situated on a commendable portion of ground, is called *nādeya*. (23)
Water that has emerged from being excavated in the earth, originating from a great mountain, pure, sweet, and delicious, is described as well-water (kaupa).
That which is naturally covered by fissured rocks,
possessing the luster of blue lotus petals,
and concealed by a canopy of creepers is known as the Caudeya [type]. 25.
Water born of marshy regions, known as *sārasa*, is heavy and slimy;
it is considered sweet, increases phlegm (*śleṣman*), and provokes wind (*vāta*) and the other humors. (26)
(4) Or, a being situated in solitude by a river or a preeminent mountain,
covered by a canopy of creepers, is designated as a *tāḍāga*. 27.
Water that originates from the earth is traditionally held to be located in a commendable region, not stagnant for many years, and to be astringent, sweet, and delicious.
Water from mountain springs is known to be light, cool, pure, and sweet; it originates on mountain peaks and is touched by wind, cold, and heat. (29)
These [substances], when not defiled by buffaloes, horses, camels, cattle, deer, goats, elephants, and so forth, should be poured into earthen vessels.
For all water born of space is inferred to be sweet;
indeed, that which is earthly is distinguished by those who know tastes according to its portion of earth.
In those that are red, pigeon-colored, yellow, pale, white, and black, [the humors] are characterized by pungent, sour, bitter, alkaline, astringent, sweet, and so forth. (32)
Now, the qualities of river water and others:
River water increases wind, is parching, stimulates digestion, is light, and is scraping.
Tank water increases wind, is sweet, astringent, and pungent in its post-digestive effect. (33)
Vāpya (watermelon) removes wind and phlegm, is alkaline, pungent, and increases bile.
Cauṇḍaya (cucumber) stimulates the digestive fire, is dry, sweet, and likewise generates phlegm. // 34 //
Water originating from springs is a destroyer of phlegm, stimulates digestion, is beneficial for the heart, and is light; it contains alkaline salts and increases pitta.
Water from wells destroys phlegm and likewise conquers vata. (35)
Water from natural springs is known to be sweet, pacifying for pitta, and non-burning;

water from irrigated fields is sweet in taste, heavy in digestion, and increases the doshas upon digestion. (It is declared to be heavy in its post-digestive effect and aggravating to the humors. // 36 //

In the same way, the marshy meat is specified as being particularly prone to defects; whereas the meat of wild animals (*jāṅgala*) removes all defects, is pleasing to the heart, and is faultless. (Ap 5, 37)
Well water quenches thirst, removes fatigue, and increases pleasure.
(The water of marshy regions is said to increase phlegm and aggravate disorders of fat.
Water from ordinary sources is digestive, sweet, cooling, and light. (38)
Thus ends the section on water common to both dry and marshy lands.
Now, regarding the rules for drinking water according to the seasons: well-water or spring-water is appropriate during the springtime, and that same [well-water] is suitable in the summer.
In the autumn season, one may enjoy all waters— whether from the clouds raining at the proper time, or from wells, or again from the thick clouds, or those belonging to lakes and ponds—
when their impurities have been shaken away by the rays of the sun and moon and by the wind.
That water which is unmanifest in taste and smell, which is praised, and which wards off wind and heat—that pure water is wholesome; otherwise, one should drink boiled water. 40.
One should worship the lake whose waters are drenched by the heat of the sun and moon day and night.
Now, as for the qualities of hot water:
that cold water, which has an unmanifest taste, is lighter than hot water and removes fainting.
[This] curd destroys phlegm, heat, thirst, and diseases of phlegm; it removes delusion and fatigue, dispels drowsiness and excessive sleep,
is pleasing to the heart, sweet, provides manifold benefits, promotes memory, and cuts through the flood of burning sensations.
Thus, for those with short lifespans, this is the sustainer of the body, the reviver, and the very life itself. // 41 //
Now, the characteristics of censured water: it is mixed with feces, urine, grass, and *nīlikā* plants; it is hot, turbid, frothy, graspable by the teeth, out of season, salty, and covered with moss.

One should never drink water that is mixed with spider webs, excessively heavy, turbid with masses of leaves and mud, or obscured by the rays of the moon and sun, for it is always full of defects. (Ap 6) 45 //
Now, the characteristics of water fit for consumption:
Water that is clear, sweet, pleasing to the heart, wholesome, nourishing, and light; water originating from a single source and always drawn from the same place is fit for consumption. (43)

Now, the benefits of drinking water at the end of the night [are as follows]: it cures cough, asthma, diarrhea, fever, skin eruptions (kiṭibha), stiffness of the waist, abdomen, and back, as well as urinary retention,
abdominal diseases, hemorrhoids, swelling, worms, vomiting, and diseases of the ears, nose, and eyes.

Furthermore, whatever other diseases of a living being there may be, caused by wind, bile, depletion, or phlegm, those various ailments are removed by drinking milk at the end of the night through the practice of regular habituation. 44.
If a wise man drinks eight handfuls of water every day,
he will become as strong as nine elephants and live for a hundred years.
Now, regarding the qualities of water drunk through the nose:
indeed, that man who, having risen every morning when the thick night has passed, regularly drinks water through the nostrils;
He becomes full of wisdom, endowed with the eye like that of Tārkṣya, free from wrinkles and grey hair, and liberated from all diseases. // 46 //
Now, the procedure for the use of water for the protection of the eyes:

That person who, having filled his mouth with cool water, daily sprinkles his two eyes with water at the three times of the day, will certainly never experience the distress caused by eye diseases. (47)
Water that is not to be taken is that which has been placed in a new earthen jar, heated by the rays of the sun,
enjoyed at night by the moonbeams, and stirred by a gentle breeze.

One should partake of that water which is cool, possesses the luster of a broken gem, and—due to its lightness—inspires no suspicion; it is fragrant with the scent of *pāṭalī*, blue lotus, and *ketakī* flowers.

O you who are like a whirlwind of ash from the wandering forest of Rudra’s matted locks, whose shimmering spray of droplets spreads across the slopes of the breasts of celestial beauties emerging [from the water],
and who washes the vast expanse of the sky with torrents of rain!
Let the water of the Gaṅgā be brought— water that destroys every sin without exception and is dense with the breaking of lofty waves.
Now, the qualities of boiled warm water: it is wholesome, a digestive stimulant, a promoter of digestion, very light, a remover of asthma and cough,
a pacifier of hiccup, flatulence, and acute fever, a destroyer of phlegm, and a conqueror of wind.

Water boiled and then cooled is declared to be beneficial for the throat; it purifies the stomach and bladder, removes pain in the heart and flanks, and cures abdominal tumors, loss of appetite, and catarrh.

In diseases where pitta is predominant, in pitta disorders, in cases of pitta-blood and kapha-pitta [disorders], in fainting, vomiting, fever, burning sensations, thirst, dyspnea, and diarrhea. // 52 //

Water that has been boiled and then cooled is always recommended for those with depleted bodily constituents (*dhātu*), those afflicted by poison, and especially for those with *sannipāta* disorders, as well as for consumption and eye diseases. (54) Now, the qualities of water according to the distinction of the time of drinking:
The four qualities of water—chatrā, amṛta, viṣa, and vajra—are [to be taken] at that very time, at dawn, or with meals when one has not yet eaten. (55)
Drinking warm water at night quickly digests undigested food;
however, during the rainy season, water should not be taken from natural sources, for such water is full of defects and harmful.
Now, the qualities of boiled water:
when one-quarter remains, it is light and stimulates the digestive fire in cases of phlegm.
But water that has been heated during the day will become heavy by night.
Water boiled and then cooled destroys the three doṣas; however, that same water, if left overnight, produces doṣas.
When reduced to one-quarter of its original volume, it destroys the doṣas; when reduced by half, it conquers vāta.
That which is boiled at night indeed acquires heaviness by day.
Now, regarding the prohibition against drinking cold water in cases such as pain in the sides:
"In cases of pain in the sides, catarrh, wind-diseases, and throat-obstruction. (58)
One should strictly avoid cold water in cases of flatulence, constipation, recent purification, acute fever, hiccups, and when there is excessive oleation or pitta. (59)

Now, the method for drinking small amounts of water in cases of abdominal tumors (gulma) and so forth: it was taught [by the Sage] for abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (agnimāndya), wasting (kṣaya), abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara), weak digestive fire, flatulence (ādhmātaka), swelling (śopha), anemia (pāṇḍu), and the seizure of the throat (galagraha). (In the case of wounds and diseases: [the same applies].
In cases of delusion (or fainting), eye diseases, wind-disorders, loss of appetite, diarrhea, phlegm-related ailments, skin diseases, and catarrh;
One should drink water that is warm, very cold, boiled and cooled, or even a small amount of plain water. // 60 //
One should drink very cold water before food to prevent indigestion;
however, if indigestion has already occurred, one may drink cold water again as desired.
Now, regarding the qualities of water cooled by fire:
water in which a clod of earth has been quenched by contact with a heated iron ball removes all defects, is wholesome, and always brings about freedom from disease.
(Āp 9) Now follows the praise of water:
in some places it is warm, in some cold, and in some it is boiled and cooled.
In some cases it is combined with medicine, while in others water is prohibited.
One who is thirsty falls into delusion; through delusion, one gives up one's life.
Therefore, even a very small amount should be given; water is never to be withheld from anyone.
Water is the life-force of living beings, for the entire universe is indeed composed of it; therefore, even when there is an extreme abundance, water is never withheld anywhere.
Cold water is beneficial in cases of fainting, pitta-related disorders, heat, burning sensations, diarrhea, alcoholism, giddiness, exhaustion, and asthma.
One may drink thousands of jars [of water] as long as the sun has not set;
once the lord of day has set, a single drop becomes a jar.
Water taken during indigestion acts as medicine; water taken after digestion bestows strength;
water with a meal is like nectar; but at night, water is like poison. (62)
Food is not properly digested from drinking excessive water, yet that same fault arises from abstaining from water altogether;
therefore, a person should drink water in small amounts repeatedly to increase the digestive fire. (70)
When one's heart and throat are parched by hunger, one should not eat many morsels at first; rather, one should drink cool water in the proper measure.
By this, there shall be purification of the heart and throat; food descends easily, and whatever food is taken mixed with unctuous substances will result in nourishment.
At the beginning, one should eat soft food and not drink much water;
in the middle, however, when eating solid food, it is recommended to drink as much water as desired. (Ap 10, 73)
A person should eat liquid food first, solid food in the middle, and liquid food again at the end; one who follows this regimen is never deprived of health. (74)
In the same way, water drunk at the end of a meal bestows strength;
however, while a substance taken after eating passes through the body, one should drink that [water] only in moderation. (75)
Water at the beginning destroys the fire; later, at the end, it increases phlegm; but when drunk in the middle, it brings the happiness of equilibrium. Its application is desired only once. (76)
To one who has thoroughly understood the true nature of reality, this water is both nectar and poison;
for that which is nectar when consumed with reason becomes poison when drunk without it. (77)
One should remain well-established, filling two parts of the belly with food,
one part with water, and the fourth part indeed for the movement of air.
At every morsel, one should always drink cool water;
food combined with plenty of water causes the digestive fire to digest quickly. (79)

Therefore, one should drink [the medicine] in very small quantities at the beginning, in a measure that provides satisfaction in the middle, and in full dose at the end; thus a person is not afflicted by diseases. (80)
It was perfumed with fresh flowers, such as the *pāṭalī* and *campaka*.
One should always drink cool water that is wholesome, fragrant, and pleasing to the heart.
(11) Water that is easily accessible, scented with lotus stalks and pieces of lotus fibers, and infused with camphor— this is always to be drunk by men. (82)
In summer and autumn, men may drink water according to their own desire;
at other times, it increases [the humors] for a kalpa— [though this is only a slight exaggeration]— one should drink it only out of fear of wind and phlegm.
Furthermore, even without food, a living being might sustain its life for a long time;
however, one afflicted by thirst in the absence of water is deprived of life in an instant. // 84 //
When food is combined with milk at the beginning, middle, and end of a meal, the qualities of emaciation, the curability of emaciation, and likewise corpulence arise respectively. // 85 //
"Drink, drink! Water, water! In autumn and in spring! Do not drink, do not drink! Water, water! In autumn and in spring! // 86 //
Thus ends the section on the qualities of water in the *Āyurvedamahodadhi* composed by Śrī Suṣeṇa.
Now begins the section on wood and hot water:
Water heated with *gandharvahastaka* wood and duly consecrated destroys misfortune (*alakṣmī*) and bile disorders (*raktapitta*), and it clarifies the bodily humors (*doṣas*). (1)
Water boiled with bhallātaka fruits and wood is auspicious water;
it removes wind and phlegm, is wholesome, and increases vitality and virility. (2)
Water heated with wood produced from the *pālāśa* or *udumbara* trees is auspicious;
it removes itching and sores, and increases the blood, strength, and virility. (3)
Water from a pond heated with wood from the *jambū*, *kapittha*,
and *āmra* trees bestows intelligence and strength, promotes virility, and destroys the defects caused by worms.
Water originating from a pond, heated with wood from the *udumbara* tree,
is prescribed as a remover of phlegm (*kapha*) and a destroyer of the [other] humors (*doṣas*). (5)
This water, heated with sticks of khadira wood, destroys *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders); it is said to be the best for providing nourishment during the summer. (6)

Water from rivers or the ocean that has been heated with the fruits of *kadamba* and *nimba* is wholesome; it removes the bodily humors (*doṣa*), and destroys itching and hemorrhagic disorders (*raktapitta*). // 7 //
Water boiled with *dhātrī* and *dāru*, when heated, is excellent for washing away impurities; it is supreme in removing wind and bile, and is a foremost elixir (*rasāyana*).
Water from a well heated with the wood of *puṣkara* (or *madhuka*) is excellent for removing wind and bile, and is a supreme elixir. (9)
It is supremely beneficial for disorders of the *grahaṇī*, anemia, heart disease, cough, and asthma.
Water produced from camphor (*karpūra*), *karkandhu*, and *dāru* wood, when heated, is auspicious; it is the best water, known as *nādeya*.
And the location of the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni) has been demonstrated by Suśruta. // 10 //
Water from a spring heated separately with the wood of sallakī, śāka, and niryāsa would produce excellent emesis; [otherwise, it] would generate many diseases. // 11 //
Water that has been continuously heated with wood of the *vaṭa* and *arjuna* trees generates strength and intelligence;
this was demonstrated by Maitreya. (12)
Tarkārī destroys wind, while [the former] increases itching and skin disorders. Fresh water, when well-heated, is beneficial for washing away impurities. (13)
Thus ends the section on wood and heated water.
regarding the distinctions of qualities based on the difference of vessels:
honey that is very sweet in taste is cool when ripened in a golden vessel.
It pacifies the three humors, produces vigor, strength, and intelligence, and is auspicious. // 1 //
And that water which comes from a vessel of glass, being slimy and sweet in taste, increases phlegm in its potency and augments the digestive fire, feces, and wind. (2)

The water in the Ghoṣapātra region is pungent in its post-digestive effect, heavy, and increases bile and phlegm; it is beneficial for strength when [the digestive fire] is increased, provided it is taken at the appropriate time (or, in the case of an increase, according to the specific occasion of distress). // 3 //
Drinking water from a falling stream, placing very cold water upon the nose, inhaling it, and sprinkling it upon the eyes— these are beneficial for pacifying the three *doṣas*. // 4 //
Water that is lukewarm and once bitter to the taste when placed in a copper vessel increases pitta and vāta; when it is old, it destroys feces and wind (or causes their aggravation). // 5 //
Water processed with brass is pungent, destroys phlegm (kapha),
increases bile (pitta), is sharp and hot, and aggravates urinary diseases.

Milk kept in an iron vessel and spoiled milk causes internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), but they are excellent for pacifying itching and the three doṣas [and for curing the defects of intoxication and stimulating the digestive fire]. // 7 //
Iron vessels heated [with medicinal substances] are said to cause itching and weak digestion,
yet they are beneficial for the evacuation of impurities and the cleansing of the internal receptacles.
Excellent water heated in a vessel made of honey-wood or udumbara is said to bestow beauty upon the body when there is pitta,
yet it causes a temporary dulling of the digestive fire. (9)
(Āp 14) Water heated in an earthen vessel is beneficial for washing away impurities;
it restores the equilibrium of the bodily constituents and increases vitality, strength, and vigor. // 10 //
Thus ends the procedure for the perfuming of vessels in the Great Ocean of Āyurveda composed by Suṣeṇa.
Now the qualities of milk are being described.
Even there, since only those derived from cows and buffaloes are suitable for constant use, their essential nature alone is first investigated.

Cow's snow (ice) is indeed most pure as milk; it bestows life, subdues bile and wind, acts as an elixir, improves the complexion, makes the hair beautiful, and is a constant cause of health for men. (1)
Milk is directly life itself; being congenial to one's birth, it is long-life-giving when warm from the cow, or when heated.
Taken in the morning, in the evening, at the conclusion of sexual intercourse, or after a meal, it makes the body habituated to its qualities. (2)
Now, regarding the specific qualities of the milk according to the specific colors of cows:
the milk of white cows destroys wind (vāta), that of black cows destroys bile (pitta), and that of red-colored cows destroys phlegm (kapha); however, the milk of a Kapilā cow destroys all three.
It is cooling, sweet, and unctuous; it is the supreme subduer of vāta and pitta; it is aphrodisiac, vitalizing, pleasing to the heart, a destroyer of kapha, and a rejuvenative elixir. // 4 //
When cooked, it has a sweet taste, is pure, restores strength depleted by consumption, alleviates asthma and cough, and removes the three types of fatigue and intoxication. (Ap 15, 5)
Cow’s milk is praised for chronic fever, dysuria, and internal hemorrhaging; it is purifying and a means of producing strength and nourishment. (6)
Cow’s milk is the best for longevity, being inexhaustible and a producer of luster and charm; it [removes] the blood,
bile, fatigue, and intoxication of those [bees].
It removes consumption, misfortune, abdominal tumors, menorrhagia, artificial poisons, and anemia; it pacifies dysuria, phlegm, fever, edema, and splenic enlargement.
It quickly pacifies thirst, fainting from fat, fever, and even wind disorders.
Now, regarding the specific qualities of particular vessels:
milk [heated] in copper removes wind (vāta), in gold it destroys bile (pitta), in silver it removes phlegm (śleṣman), and in bell-metal it clarifies the blood. // 8 //
Thus ends [the section on] cow's milk.
Now, regarding buffalo milk:
Buffalo milk bestows strength, complexion, and vitality; it induces sleep and increases the power of digestion and semen.
It pacifies a sharp digestive fire, is sweet in taste and post-digestive effect, and provides nourishment. (1)
It removes fatigue for one whose body is exhausted by physical exertion, dispels wind disorders, and bestows sexual pleasure upon even an old man who is free from desire. // 2 //
"It is strengthening even for a youth, and especially bestows the fulfillment of desires.
Thus ends the section on buffalo meat.
Now, regarding goat's milk:
because goats have few desires and because they consume pungent and bitter substances, [goat's milk is wholesome].
Milk removes all diseases when it is not consumed in excessive quantities and when one avoids physical exertion.
Goat’s milk increases digestive fire and strength; it is supreme for removing consumption, cough, and cardiac instability.
It quickly removes *raktapitta* and is indeed declared beneficial in cases of hemorrhagic dysentery (*raktātisāra*). (Ap 16) 4. [sic]
Now, regarding camel’s milk:
camel’s milk removes swelling caused by sleep and is commended for excessive bile and phlegm, as well as hemorrhoids.
It destroys abdominal distension, is excellent for treating abdominal enlargements (udara), and is indeed praised at all times as a destroyer of parasites. // 5 //
Now, regarding the milk of a mare: it is warm, derived from a single-hoofed animal, strengthening, and it removes asthma and wind disorders.
It is sweet and sour in taste, parching, with a salty aftertaste, and light.
(The milk of a donkey and a horse.
Now, human breast-milk.
Breast milk is sweet, has an astringent aftertaste, is cooling, beneficial for nasal medication and eye-drops, vitalizing, light, and digestive-stimulating.
Now, regarding elephant milk:
that of the female elephant is sweet, aphrodisiac, with an astringent aftertaste, heavy, and unctuous.
It bestows fortitude, is cooling, beneficial for the eyes, and increases strength.
(Ap 17) Now, the general qualities of milk: Milk is generally proclaimed to be moistening and heavy when raw.
One should know that very [milk] as being more nourishing, heavy, satiating, and strengthening. // 8 //
Except for the breast milk of a woman, which is indeed raw, unrefined, and possesses the heat of digestion—being nectar-like milk—it is called "the opposite" (otherwise). 9.
Now, regarding milk that is censured:
that which has an undesirable odor, is sour, discolored, or tasteless, is to be avoided.
One should not consume milk that is salty or coagulated;
nor should one eat milk during the day, and if one does eat it, one must not sleep.
If one should sleep, life will come to an end; therefore, milk is nectar during the day.
Now, the qualities of water at various stages: Water poured while still warm (*dhāroṣṇa*) is nectar-like and wholesome; water cooled by the stream (*dhārāśīta*) aggravates the three *doṣas*;
boiled water that has been cooled (*śṛta-śīta*) destroys the three *doṣas*; and water that is cool yet warm (*śītoṣṇa*) conquers *kapha* and *vāta*. (12)
Furthermore, sheep's milk is most wholesome when boiled and heated;
goat's milk is indeed beneficial when boiled and cooled; buffalo's milk is wholesome when well-cooled from the stream, and cow's milk is likewise beneficial when warm from the stream.
Furthermore:
Buffalo milk alleviates bile; sheep's milk alleviates wind;
cow's milk removes wind and bile; and goat's milk destroys the three humors. (14)
(Ap 18) Now, the qualities of milk according to the time of milking:
Generally, morning milk is heavy, causes constipation, and is cold.
And because of its gentle qualities during the night, as well as due to the absence of physical exertion; (17)
For those tormented by the sun, the afternoon meal— due to the consumption of air from physical exertion—
is indeed a remover of wind and bile, and it is beneficial for the eyes.
Now, the specific benefits of drinking milk in the forenoon and other times:
milk drunk in the forenoon is aphrodisiac, nourishing, and generates an increase in digestive fire; at midday it bestows strength and promotes sexual vigor, and it cures dysuria and urinary calculi.
Milk, which produces digestive fire in the young, strength in the aged, and carries the semen at night, pacifies many disorders and should always be consumed by living beings. (17)
Those pungent, sharp, and fierce bitter flavors that have been consumed, those sour and bitter tastes, those which are parching, alkaline, burning, drying, and extremely scorching,
and those astringent, harsh, rough, and most difficult to digest— if these are indulged in with laughter, [what will happen]?
All that, when milked and consumed at night, produces strength by its power. (18)
Now, the rule regarding the time for the transformation of milk:
After five muhūrtas, milk undergoes transformation;
at twice that time, it kills a person like poison. (19)
(Āyurveda-prakāśa 19) Now,
a further description of the qualities of milk that is warm from the udder: milk fresh from the cow's udder pacifies the provocation of the wind (*vāta*) and promotes nourishment.
It swiftly overcomes anemia and jaundice, which cause loss of vigor and distress;

it conquers burning sensations throughout the body, inflammation of the hands, feet, and eyes, an excess of bile, vitiated blood, emaciation born of digestive fire, and diseases such as *kṛcchra*. (20)
Now, the determination of the period during which boiled milk and other preparations are wholesome:
unboiled milk is wholesome for ten *ghaṭikās*, while boiled milk is wholesome for twice that duration; furthermore, milk and preparations such as meat broth are wholesome at dawn.
It should be lukewarm and rich with its own juice;
as much milk as [is required] should be consumed. // 21 //
Now, regarding the suitability and unsuitability of milk in fever:
In chronic fever where phlegm has been depleted, milk is like nectar;
yet that very same milk, when drunk during the acute stage, kills a person like poison. (22)
Therefore, one should drink milk that has been boiled, or even unboiled milk, at that very time;
or that milk which has been processed by adding one-fourth part water and then being stirred.

Therefore, that [milk] is the best among difficult-to-digest milks; it is beneficial and removes various diseases. Now follows the preparation of milk for those for whom it is unsuitable (those to whom it is not habituated).
And this, when drunk directly with milk, causes flatulence.
Having added half as much water along with ginger and long pepper, one should boil it down until only the milk remains; by drinking that, one will bring about well-being. (25)
(Ap 20) Now follows the determination of the times for drinking according to the different types of milk, such as that of cows and others:
in the forenoon, one may drink buffalo milk with sugar, or according to one's own preference?
For those whose equilibrium is always maintained—

[it should be noted that the reading "cow's milk may be taken in the forenoon, while buffalo's milk with sugar is wholesome in the afternoon, and [other milks] are always beneficial according to one's constitution" is what should be recited].
Either at the beginning or at midday—(therefore, both at the start and in the middle)—or sometimes at the edge of the village. // 26 //
All that remains of the meal,
however, should always be drunk as milk by men; it is praised as such.
Now, furthermore, regarding the description of the qualities of milk that has been boiled and cooled:
milk that is boiled and then cooled destroys *pitta*; when cooked [and served] warm, it removes *kapha*;
however, that which is simply cooled without being boiled brings about the disorder of *viṣṭambha* (constipation/distension).

Milk that is warm from the udder is nectar-like; it removes fatigue, induces sleep, bestows luster, quenches thirst, promotes corpulence, increases the digestive fire, is delicious, and pacifies the three doṣas. (27)
Now follows the prohibition against consuming milk together with poisoned food.
One should consume milk, but neither with wheat-based food nor with flour-based food;
one should not eat it with curd or with salt.
Neither with black gram nor with mung beans, nor with molasses or fruit; neither with tubers from the ground nor with leafy vegetables, nor with fish, meat, and the like. (29)
Now, the qualities of milk-rice (pāyasa):
One should eat milk-rice with proper moderation; for when it is cooked, one should consume it in equal measure.
It is aphrodisiac, pleasing to the heart, wholesome, and it destroys bile and digestive fire disorders. 30.
(Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 21) Now follows the prohibition against drinking water at the three times of day even for one who maintains the sacred fires and so forth.

Due to its unctuousness, heaviness, and dullness, one should not drink milk at the three times of day; this applies whether one has a balanced digestive fire, or otherwise a weak or irregular fire. (31)
But for one with a sharp digestive fire, there is inference from that [experience]:
one with a sharp fire may drink even buffalo milk twice a day;
when his fire digests the bodily constituents (dhātus), he does not become moistened by it. // 32 //
Now, furthermore, is the praise of milk:
Milk is beneficial and the best of rejuvenators (*rasāyana*); milk is for the sake of the body’s form, complexion, strength, and longevity.
Indeed, milk brings long life to men; milk is the supreme establisher of strength. (33)
Milk indeed is both stimulating and digestive; milk that is warm is a purifier of impurities.
Milk that is both hot and cold acts as a healer of fractures, while milk that is lukewarm destroys morbid humors.
Now follows the prohibition against consuming milk together with fish and other such items:
Milk consumed with fish, meat, molasses, mung beans, and radishes brings about leprosy;
when consumed with vegetables, rose-apple, wine, and the like, it quickly kills the ignorant man, just like a serpent. (35)
(Ap 22) Now follows the procedure for drinking milk with various medicinal juices.
Edible foods are not incompatible when taken with milk; for example, among sour things, the *āmalaka* fruit is wholesome, and among sweet things, sugar is wholesome. (36)
One should employ *paṭola* among the groups of bitter vegetables (*śāka-tikta-vargeṣu*), and one should cook fresh ginger (*ārdraka*) in the pungent category (*kaṭuke*).
Among astringents, barley is the best, and among salts, rock salt.
Thus ends the section on milks in the *Āyurvedamahodadhi* composed by Suṣeṇa.
Now, the qualities of cow's curd.
Among those, cow's curd is very cooling, digestive, strength-promoting, wind-alleviating, sweet, dry, and pleasing to the mind. (38)
Cow’s curd is unctuous, sweet in its post-digestive effect, digestive-stimulant, strength-promoting, wind-alleviating, purifying, and provides a relish for food. (39)
In cases of loss of appetite, chronic rhinitis, dysuria, cold-fever, and irregular fever, as well as in hemorrhoids and disorders of the digestive tract, cow's curd is always recommended. (40)
Now, regarding the merits and demerits of consuming curd according to the distinction of seasons:
in autumn, summer, and spring, curd is censured and causes harm;
however, in winter, the cool season, and the rainy season, it yields beneficial results.
(23) Now, the qualities of buffalo curd:
it is sweet in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), aphrodisiac, and clarifies the blood and bile (*rakta-pitta*).
Buffalo curd, in particular, increases phlegm (balāsa).
It is unctuous, sweet, and cooling; it is supreme for bestowing strength and complexion, aphrodisiac, promotes fat, is delicious, destroys fatigue, and subdues Vāta. (43)
Buffalo milk increases phlegm and undigested matter (āmavardhana), as well as providing nourishment;
it is purifying, cools fever, and increases luster.
Buffalo curd causes phlegm and quickly diminishes the digestive fire due to its heaviness;
however, when that buffalo curd is sprinkled with pungent spices, it attains lightness.
Buffalo curd.
Now, the qualities of goat's curd: goat's curd is sour,
destroys phlegm and wind, subdues wind, and is hot.
It is beneficial for dyspnea associated with cough,
and it kindles the digestive fire; it is aphrodisiac, nourishing, bestows digestive power, luster, and strength, and destroys all diseases in cases of hemorrhoids.
This is always beneficial for living beings suffering from dysentery. // 46 //
Goat’s curd alleviates cough and dyspnea, stimulates the appetite, destroys edema and diarrhea, is fiery in nature, and specifically destroys all the [three] doṣas. (47)
Now, the qualities of sheep's curd:
Sheep's curd is unctuous, sweet, heavy, and increases pitta and kapha;
it is wholesome in cases of pure vāta disorders, as well as in swelling and vātarakta. (48)
(Āpastamba Śulba Sūtra 24) Now, the qualities of the horse:
the vigor born of the steed, its even gait, its strength and color, and its sweat— these perish when it suffers from heat (or heaviness).
It is digestive, excessively dosha-increasing, always beneficial for the eyes, and it agitates the wind (vāta). 49.
Now, the qualities of camel curd:
it destroys wind, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, and worms; it is pungent in its post-digestive effect and slightly bitter;
it is alkaline, sour, and pungent, and it destroys skin diseases and intestinal worms.
And it is strengthening, nourishing, and acts quickly.
Now, the qualities of elephant's curd: it is heavy, hot, and astringent, and it removes phlegm and urine disorders. Now, the qualities of woman's curd:
It is unctuous, sweet in its post-digestive effect, strengthening, nourishing, and heavy.
The curd from a black cow (*dadhi-kātra*) is beneficial for the eyes, destroys all defects, and possesses the highest qualities. // 52 //
Curd that is light in digestion, destroys phlegm (balāsa), is hot in potency, and alleviates bile (pitta);
it is compatible with astringent tastes and increases the fecal matter of women. (53)
One should desire it with restraint; curd that has been stirred with *maska* and mixed with sesame and milk is known as *gurudadhi*. //54//
The water that remains at the bottom of curdled milk is called *mastu*;
that which is produced from boiled milk is known as *śṛta-dadhi*, and it is considered to be of excellent quality.
It removes wind and bile, stimulates the appetite, and increases the strength of the bodily tissues (*dhātu*), the digestive fire (*agni*), and physical vigor.
(Āyurveda-prakāśa 25) Now, the qualities of curd-sugar:
a piece of curd is heavy, aphrodisiac, and known to increase strength.
And cloth-water, having been squeezed out, also destroys phlegm and bile.
Now, the qualities of insubstantial curd (*asāradadhi*):

Insubstantial curd is parching, constipating, causes the retention of feces (*viṣṭambhi*), increases wind (*vātala*), stimulates digestion (*dīpanīya*), is very light, slightly astringent, and provides relish (*ruciprada*). // 56 //
Now, the qualities of whey:
Whey removes thirst and fatigue; it is cooling and purifies the channels.
It is sour, astringent, and sweet; it is non-aphrodisiac and alleviates phlegm and wind. // 57 //
Now, the general qualities of curd:

It is sour in taste and post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), heavy, a subduer of *vāta*, cooling, and an absorbent; it is declared to be beneficial in disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*), and it removes difficulties in the passage of feces and urine.
It is strengthening, but it generates swelling, phlegm, and sluggish digestion; it provides blood and relieves cough, dryness, anorexia, and coryza.
It is most effective for intermittent fever and cold-fever caused by that [wind]. (58)
Curd is always recommended for disorders of the digestive tract, catarrh, dysuria, intermittent fever, anorexia, and weak digestion. (59)
One should not eat food that is devoid of salt, black pepper, ghee, sugar, mung beans, and the juice of *dhātrī* flowers; nor should one eat such food constantly.
Furthermore, one should not consume curd in autumn, in spring, during the hot season, at night, when there is a disorder of phlegm (*kapha*), or in cases of bile (*pitta*) or jaundice. // 6 //
Cardamom, rock salt, sugar, black pepper, emblic myrobalan, and jaggery, along with ghee and an excellent soup of mung beans, constitute wholesome food; one should partake of it together with curd.
It is neither too hot nor excessively slimy; it is beneficial during autumn, summer, and spring,
yet otherwise it causes bile and blood disorders, fever, leprosy, dizziness, and erysipelas.
Curd mixed with the three pungents (trikaṭuka) and powdered black mustard (rājikā) removes phlegm, subdues wind, kindles the digestive fire,
and is wholesome to be consumed during the cold and chilly seasons.
He becomes one with a very firm body, possessed of beauty and endowed with strength. // 62 //

It produces leanness of the body and beauty for men; curd mixed with jaggery, made lukewarm, properly strained through a clean cloth by the graceful hands of a young woman, and fumigated with incense.
Mixed with the powder of viśvājājī from the cool-rayed moon [candana],
it removes phlegm, subdues wind, and kindles the digestive fire.
And that which is beneficial should be consumed during the cold season of frost; thus one becomes possessed of a very firm body, handsome in form, and endowed with vital strength.
It was attended to and massaged with even greater luxuries. // 63 //
Fresh curd is unwholesome for those seeking nourishment through wholesome diet, yet it bestows strength, is highly aphrodisiac, produces fat, stimulates digestion,
alleviates phlegm, and does not excessively aggravate bile, provided there is a presence of wind (vāta).
Therefore, its sweetness should be enjoyed here incessantly because of its transformation into acidity.
One should eat this when it is sweet and always avoid it when it is excessively sour;
sweet curd is a destroyer of disease, while excessively sour curd is a cause of disease.
Thus ends the chapter on curd (*dadhivarga*) in the *Āyurvedamahodadhi*, composed by Suśeṇa.
(Ap 27) Now, the qualities of *mastu* are described.
It provides purity to the channels, manifests luster, and quickly kindles the digestive fire; having purified the impurities, it forcibly digests various kinds of food that are hot,
sour, or astringent, light, and fragrant in taste, while removing colic and constipation.
The cream of curd (mastu) is excellent and highly praised for disorders of phlegm and wind, for pain, and for the retention of urine. // 1 //
Light food provides relish and promotes digestion; it removes fatigue, is strengthening, astringent, laxative, and stimulates the desire for more food.
It cures thirst, abdominal enlargement, splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, and swelling;
it facilitates purification after vomiting, subdues phlegm and wind, and alleviates flatulence and colic.
Buttermilk made from *pāṇḍu* [grain] is commended for alleviating urinary disorders and abdominal tumors; it is light and wholesome. // 2 //
Because it is light, because it stimulates digestion, because it destroys constipation and flatulence, and because it purifies the channels, buttermilk causes curd to be digested. (3)
Thus ends the section on mastu in the Great Ocean of Ayurveda.
Now the qualities of buttermilk are described.
Ghola, mathita, udaśvit, and takra—these are said to be the four kinds [of buttermilk].

What is flavorful yet waterless? What is sweet yet devoid of water? What is churned yet without water? [The answer is: "Flavorful yet waterless" refers to the primordial [state]; "devoid of essence" refers to that which has had its flavor extracted; and "without water" refers to that which has been churned.
They say that water with half a foot of liquid is *udaśvit*, and that water with half a foot of liquid is *takra*.
And for each of the four, the narrative should be understood with diligent effort. // 2 //
That which has flavor but no water is known as *nirjala*; *mathita* is churned [curd] devoid of flavor;
*pādodaka* is [curd with] one-quarter water, while *udaśvit* would be [curd with] half water—that is *takra*. // 3 //
(Ap 28) Now,
the qualities of buttermilk made from cow’s milk, buffalo’s milk, and goat’s milk:
cow’s buttermilk is digestive, promotes intellect, and overcomes the three *doṣas* as well as hemorrhoids.
Buffalo buttermilk increases phlegm; goat buttermilk is light and removes the three doshas. // 4 //
It destroys abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, edema, anemia, and consumption.
Now, the qualities of the various types of *takra* (buttermilk): *ghola* removes wind and bile; *mathita* cures dyspnea and removes phlegm.
Buttermilk that contains more whey destroys bile and phlegm; it removes the three doṣas.
The sages declare this buttermilk to be excellent for those with weak digestion and loss of appetite, as well as for other diseases; therefore, it is the best sustenance for living beings.
Now, the praise of buttermilk:
Just as nectar is preeminent among the gods, so they say that buttermilk is [preeminent] for men on earth.
It immediately subdues wind by its acidity, bile by its sweetness, and phlegm by its astringency. (7)
It destroys wind and phlegm, [removes worms], cuts through dysuria and urinary stones,

cures urinary retention, pacifies urinary disorders (prameha), and removes splenic pain and abdominal tumors; it eradicates hemorrhoids, abdominal enlargement, anemia, and the severe pains of chronic stomach ailments.
Buttermilk is a digestive stimulant and a carminative; it is extremely light and always wholesome for living beings. // 8 //

One should always drink buttermilk in cases of diarrhea with undigested matter, dysentery, fever caused by wind, anemia, jaundice, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargement, wind-pain, and loss of appetite. (9)
Buttermilk is sweet, astringent, and sour in taste; it is light, hot, and beneficial as food.

Milk should be consumed as it pacifies abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and chronic colic; it removes vomiting and excessive salivation; it conquers thirst, anorexia, urinary disorders, edema, and skin diseases; it destroys phlegm and lethargy; it cures urinary ailments and fever; and it alleviates pain arising from the improper use of oleation therapy. (10)
Butter-milk is recommended during the cold season, in cases of weak digestion, those arising from phlegm, jaundice, obstruction of the channels, and when the digestive fire is impaired. (11)
Furthermore, that which is sweet is primarily provocative of phlegm;
however, if it is sour, it subdues wind and bile, though it always produces bile.
The specific preparation of buttermilk according to the particular humor involved:
it is sour and combined with rock salt for Vāta; it is sweet and with sugar for Pitta.
In cases of kapha and pitta, or even in kapha, one should drink buttermilk combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and alkali.
This very [substance], ghee, when its heat has never departed, causes thickness and removes wind (*vāta*). It is always thus.
Ghee (*sarpiḥ*).
That [milk] should be consumed together with a decoction of *adhuka* and mung beans, avoiding the seasons of spring and autumn. // 14 //
The wise say that butter churned at the door of fresh cream is excellent;
however, that which has been churned for a long time causes the recurrence of a man's ailments. 15.
Contraindications regarding buttermilk in specific diseases:
One should never administer buttermilk in cases of chest wounds, nor during the hot season, nor when the patient is weak;
nor in cases of fainting, vertigo, or burning sensations, nor in diseases characterized by blood and pitta. (16)
(Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.30) Praise of Buttermilk:
It has a luster like the moon or jasmine, resembling a conch shell, and is churned by the pure hands of young women.
O King, drink this well-ripened, fragrant wood-apple juice mixed with buttermilk, which removes all ailments.

Churned cow's milk product (mathita) is called *ghola* when it is liquid and stirred with whey (*mastu*); when it is white, struck by a stick, and thick, it is proclaimed by its respective names. (18)
This [mixture] with twice as much water and white [in color] is known as *ardhodaka*; but buttermilk (*takra*) with one-third part [of water] added is known simply as *mathita*.
The water on top of buttermilk is celebrated as *udaśvit*;
the water on top of curd is celebrated as *mastu*.
Buttermilk is constipating, increases wind, is dry, and is difficult to digest; it produces strength.
Maṇḍa is lighter than buttermilk, while kūcikā is like curdled buttermilk.
Because Śatakratu [Indra] regarded the absence of ritual as the essence of ritual while drinking buttermilk, therefore buttermilk produced in heaven is difficult for Śakra to obtain. 22.
If there were buttermilk on Kailāsa, would Giriśa become dark-complexioned?
If Keśava were to experience blackness in Vaikuṇṭha even today, would he still be so?
Indra conquers out of fear of misfortune; the Lord of the Twice-born [conquers] that very [misfortune].
If there is a divine being, Gaṇa has pot-belliedness, Kubera has leprosy, and Agni has the nature of fire. // 23 //

That substance which is conch-white in color, resembling a mass of snow, possessing a lovely fragrance, very cool, as pure as the water of the Gaṅgā, shattered by the striking of a young woman’s hand against iron,
and when churned with a churning-stick, becomes foam in the form of bubbles through the force of her palm— [that is nectar].
Fortunate people drink that buttermilk, well-perfumed and resembling the qualities of nectar. // 24 //
Thus ends the section on buttermilk in the *Āyurvedamahodadhi*, composed by Suśeṇa.
(Ap 31) Now, the section on fresh butter (navanīta) is being told.

It is cooling, bestows complexion and strength, is sweet, aphrodisiac, astringent, subdues wind, removes phlegm, stimulates the appetite, is heart-pleasing, alleviates the three doṣas, and relieves pain throughout the entire body.
It pacifies cough and fatigue from travel, provides delight, bestows luster, and grants nourishment.
This freshly extracted butter, being newly drawn, removes all diseases;
(the fresh butter extracted from a cow is beneficial for the eyes and removes all humors).
Cf. Rājanighaṇṭu 15.63.
It is cooling, strengthening, sweet and sour, aphrodisiac, dispels phlegm,
destroys bile and wind,
and [is beneficial for those] emaciated by grief or consumption.
Fresh butter is wholesome for the elderly and the young when it is warmed. // 2 //

Fresh butter, whether derived from cow's milk or buffalo's milk, when recently extracted, is recommended for the young and the old; it bestows strength and increases the bodily constituents (dhātus). // 3 //
It is cooling, bestows complexion and strength, is sweet, aphrodisiac, astringent,
pleasing to the heart, and removes asthma, old age, consumption, bile, acidity, and wind; it also cures cough, hemorrhoids, and fever.
This fresh buffalo butter is a pacifier of swelling, a remover of pain in the relaxed limbs, and it shall be a destroyer of all diseases. // 4 //
Thus end the qualities of fresh butter.
Now, therefore, the qualities of ghee are described.

Among these, first are the qualities of cow's ghee: it produces intelligence, beauty, and memory; it bestows strength, wisdom, and intellect; it subdues wind (vāta), destroys fatigue, improves the voice, removes bile (pitta), and grants nourishment.

This cow's ghee, which increases the digestive fire, has a sweet post-digestive effect, is aphrodisiac, and is always cooling; it bestows strength and should be consumed immediately after it is freshly prepared. (Ap 32) // 1 //

The wise declare that cow’s ghee is like nectar; it destroys poison, benefits the eyes, promotes health, is aphrodisiac, acts as a rejuvenative, is highly purifying, and is the best of all unctuous substances.
Now, the qualities of buffalo ghee:
buffalo ghee is the best; it provides stability, bestows happiness, grants luster, subdues wind and phlegm, increases strength, and is capable of clarifying the complexion.

The fruit of the *navagavya* (the nine products of the cow) is beneficial for the eyes and pacifies disorders of the spleen (*durnāma*) and dyspepsia (*agrahaṇīvikāra*), while stimulating a sluggish digestive fire (*mandānala*).
This is heart-pleasing and captivating. // 3 //
That which is derived from buffalo is recommended for humans; it is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and relieves pain in the bladder.
That which is produced from fat causes urinary disorders and dysuria; therefore, it should be consumed constantly at all times.
The qualities of clarified butter are as follows: goat's ghee is digestive, beneficial for the eyes, and increases strength;
it is wholesome even in cases of cough, dyspnea, and wasting, and it is light when used for drinking.
The qualities of sheep's ghee:
Sheep's ghee, because of its extreme heaviness, should indeed be avoided, especially by those who are delicate.
The qualities of camel ghee are such that it immediately produces strength and nourishment, whereas that produced from a camel causes swelling and coughing.
Furthermore,
cow-derived clarified butter that has been cooked removes vomiting, bile, and phlegm; it is beneficial when taken with milk, as is the case with that from sheep.
Clarified butter from a she-goat and a she-donkey. // 7 //
Camel ghee is pungent in potency; it removes phlegm, worms, and poisons.
It is digestive, subdues kapha and vāta, and cures skin diseases, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the abdomen. // 8 //
Clarified butter processed with light and other [substances] is not provocative of pitta;
it is beneficial for kapha, vāta, disorders of the female reproductive tract, edema, and tremors. (9)
One should know that clarified butter from single-hoofed animals is light in digestion, hot in potency, astringent in taste, a destroyer of phlegm,
digestive-stimulant, and light in its effect. (10)
Clarified butter from women is beneficial for the eyes and kindles the digestive fire; it is like nectar for women, increases the bodily fire, is light in digestion, and destroys poison. 11.
The decoction of *hastinī* ghee is bitter, promotes the digestion of food, is light, and cures the obstruction of feces and urine.
Clarified butter cures elephantiasis and is effective against troublesome worms, phlegm, skin diseases, poisons, and parasites. // 12 //
(Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.34) Praising clarified butter:
it increases longevity, makes the body firm, and produces delicacy.
That which dispels the fatigue caused by physical exertion, sexual intercourse,
and wrestling is wholesome in childhood, youth, and even old age;
for a man, there is nothing else that produces corpulence like clarified butter.
That which has been declared here by those who know the Vedas and Agamas as the actual lifespan of men;

that which has been taught by physicians for the sake of elixirs (*rasāyana*) as the immediate destroyer of old age; and that which, possessing the splendor of the *Sārasvata-kalpa*, has been proclaimed by the wise for the perfection of the intellect—[all this is contained herein].
In that regard, ghee should be joyfully offered, resembling a mass of light from a single-rayed ketaka flower. (14)

The noble ones say that this ghee is extremely cooling, sweet in its qualities and its post-digestive effect, a rejuvenative for the three doshas, and it bestows luster, strength, and longevity; it is clarifying to the intellect and beneficial for the eyes. 15.

It generates an increase in vigor and luster, bestows happiness, and produces beauty; it is rightly said to destroy sin, misfortune, and fatigue, and to cure asthma, cough, indigestion, and fever arising therefrom; it also cures colic, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), diseases of the digestive tract, and pain in the hips.
It quickly destroys bile and [pain], subdues wind, and eliminates bile; it is beneficial for the voice, an antidote for hunger and dizziness, and should indeed be consumed. 16.
It is beneficial for the eyes, aphrodisiac, promotes longevity, memory, and fortitude; it pacifies and destroys the provocation of *rājayakṣmā* (consumption);
it is wholesome in cases of dryness and emaciation, removes wrinkles and graying hair, and is effective when the *sāma-doṣas* are provoked.
It is beneficial for those afflicted by spirits, insanity, intoxication, excessive darkness of vision, and epilepsy. It brings about auspiciousness and glory.
For everyone and at all times, ghee—possessing a multitude of celebrated qualities—should be wholesome and beneficial. // 17 //
Fresh urine,
purified by straining through cloth, cleanses the urinary bladder.
It increases phlegm, destroys bile, and promotes strength and nourishment. // 18 //
The ancient [Purāṇa] removes darkness of vision, dyspnea, catarrh, fever, and cough;
it destroys fainting, leprosy, poison, intoxication, possession by spirits, and epilepsy. (19)
Ghee that has been stored for ten years becomes old and possesses a pungent odor;
when it is cooled and resembles the color of lac juice, it indeed destroys the influence of serpents and seizing spirits.
It conquers chronic diseases such as intoxication, epilepsy, fainting, and those arising from the head, ears, eyes, and female genital tract; it also cleanses and heals wounds. (21)
It is especially recommended for those afflicted by epilepsy, planetary seizures, and insanity;
it possesses the aforementioned qualities in greater measure, and is like nectar itself. 22.

Having prepared the pure, freshly washed milk of healthy cows in their prime youth, cook it thoroughly in fire; that fresh butter, when refined into ghee, is fit—most certainly fit—for the consumption of the king of elephants.
Thus ends the section on clarified butter (*ghṛtavarga*) in the *Āyurvedamahodadhi* composed by Suṣeṇa.
Now, the qualities of oil (taila):
Hot in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), pungent and slightly bitter, it subdues phlegm (kapha) and wards off wind (vāta).
Oil destroys worms, bestows strength, and promotes digestion; it is the destroyer of worms, phlegm, and wind. // 1 //

Sesame oil beautifies the hair, is sweet, bitter, and astringent; it is hot and sharp, provides strength, cures disorders born of *kapha* and *vāta*, removes itching from sores, and bestows luster. (Ap 36) // 2 //
This oil produced from sesame seeds indeed removes itching, increases luster, promotes the growth of hair, heals wounds, and is beneficial for both the young and the old. (3)
They declare that oil produced from sesame seeds is wholesome neither in bile diseases nor in those arising from blood, nor in the combination of great disorders of wind;
yet it destroys all the humors when they are localized in the wind.

Mustard oil possesses sharp potency, generates much bile, causes the retention of feces and urine, and produces excessive heat; yet, when used as an ointment, it removes skin diseases such as scabies and other ailments. (5)
Mustard oil is pungent and hot; it removes phlegm, semen, and wind.
However, oil produced from eggs is sharp, hot, slimy, and foul-smelling, and it excessively aggravates the blood.
The castor oil lion alone is the conqueror of the lordly elephants of rheumatic wind that roam the forest of the body. (8)
Safflower oil destroys worms but diminishes vitality and ruins the eyes;
dates and hair cause itching in the stomach and [itching] when seen.
It pacifies the three doṣas and also subdues the wind (vāta).
An ointment made from silver-leaf oil destroys eye diseases,
cures leprosy and those afflicted by the effects of past sins, and removes all disorders of the wind (vāta).

Oil produced from nimba is pungent, sweet, cooling, beneficial for the hair, heavy, and it subdues pitta and vāta; it is neither excessively hot nor cold, and it cures worms, skin diseases, and pain. (Ap 37, 11)
Linseed oil is not beneficial for the eyes, increases pitta, and destroys vāta.
Flaxseed oil destroys kapha and pitta, is beneficial for the hair, and nourishes the eyes and ears. (12)
Castor oil is considered purgative; others are known to act like sesame oil.
Thus ends the section on oils in the Great Ocean of Ayurveda composed by Suṣeṇa.
Now the qualities of honey are described:
Honey cleanses, heals, and promotes the healing of wounds; it increases wind (*vāta*), is dry, and is astringent-sweet.
Honey-sugar possesses qualities similar to those of honey. (1)
Honey is said to destroy the three doṣas; that of another [bee] is called Śrī-saṃnipāta-lam.
It removes hiccup, asthma, phlegm, vomiting, intoxication, thirst, and poison. // 2 //
A person with excessive corpulence should drink honey mixed with water;
he becomes lean— so it is truly said.
Writing arises therein. // 3 //

In that case, an ointment beneficial for hemorrhoids is the elephant-produced [gum] (guggulu) to be licked; it increases vitality day by day. Moreover, every heavy substance is a rejuvenative (rasāyana), and the use of honey also removes cough. // 4 //
Honey is beneficial for the body; it destroys vomiting with mucus, hiccups, and diarrhea, and it cures wounds and skin diseases.
It alleviates itching and wounds; indeed, the application of honey is like divine nectar for those suffering from various ailments that require wound-healing and digestive stimulation. (5)
Whether it be stationary, mobile, or artificial, [this] removes poison;
and in that body, one becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair. (6)
It is beneficial for those who are emaciated by chest wounds, and it conquers the diseases of *pāṇḍu* and *amlapitta*.
It is also beneficial for those who are obese or suffering from black [complexion], and it is likewise beneficial in cases of blood disorders.
It is sweet when cooked and excellent as honey, yet in its post-digestive effect it is associated with the humors;
that honey arises from the intoxication of waters obstructed within the earth. (8)
The production of worms and insects occurs from long pepper taken with honey;
when sweet and sour, it is palatable, yet that honey also causes disorder of the humors.
Now the qualities of sugarcane are described.
The dark sugarcane is unctuous, nourishing, strengthening, vitalizing, sweet-tasting, and a destroyer of fatigue;
it is aphrodisiac, removes bile, fatigue, and wind, causes internal burning, and increases phlegm.
Similarly, that which is mixed with black gram (kṛṣṇa) becomes aphrodisiac, nourishing, and a destroyer of thirst and burning sensations;
it is slightly alkaline and sweet in taste, a remover of wasting diseases, yet it causes suppuration and swelling in wounds. // 2 //
Pāṇḍuka, Bhīruka, Vārāha, Śvetapotaka, Kāntāra, Tāpasekṣu, Kāṣṭhekṣu, and Vicitraka. // 3 //
The Nepalese, the Dīpyayantra, the Nīla, and that which is made from a silver casket—these are the varieties of thick [saffron]; hereafter I shall describe their qualities. (Ap 39, v. 4)
The Pauṇḍraka and Bhīruka varieties are very cool, sweet, unctuous, nourishing, and increase phlegm; they are non-burning, heavy, and aphrodisiac. (5)
Others have similar qualities; some consider vaṃśaka to be alkaline.
White pauṇḍra, however, is like vaṃśaka, though it is slightly warm and subdues wind.
The *kāntāra* variety is considered to be like sugarcane and followed by bamboo;
the *kāṣṭhekṣu* possesses these same qualities, but it aggravates the wind (*vāta*).
Sūcīpatra, nīlapatra, nīlāpa (Nepālī),
and dīrghapatraka are destroyers of vāta, destroyers of kapha and pitta, and are slightly astringent and burning. // 8 //
Sugar from the *kośātakī* plant is cooling and removes hemorrhaging (*raktapitta*) and wasting (*kṣaya*).
Its root is exceedingly sweet, and its middle portion is likewise sweet. (9)
Sugar-cane is known to be sweet at its tips; it is traditionally held to be slightly salty, increases phlegm, is non-burning, and destroys blood-bile (raktapitta). // 10 //
The juice extracted by crushing the teeth, possessing a potency equal to sugar, is proclaimed as *yāntrika*; it is heavy, causes a burning sensation, and leads to constipation. (11)
Molasses (*phāṇita*) that is matured is heavy, has a pungent taste, is unctuous, slightly sharp, alleviates *kapha* and *vāta*, and is nourishing;
it is heavy, sweet, and causes internal secretions (*abhiṣyandi*). // 12 //
It produces semen and phlegm, and especially subdues bile;
it is alkaline, sweet, increases urine excessively, purifies the blood,
restrains fat, pacifies bile, and suppresses wind while causing flatulence.

It generates phlegm, promotes nourishment, is strengthening, always maintains health, subdues wind, and pacifies irregular fever and acid dyspepsia; however, it should never be consumed in excess. // 13 //

The qualities of sugar-candy and related products: sugar-candy (*matsyaṇḍikā*) is superior to candied sugar (*khaṇḍa*), granulated sugar (*śarkarā*), and refined sugar (*pāṣāṇa*). It is smeared [with medicinal properties].
Sugar is heavy, sweet with a progressively sweeter post-digestive effect, aphrodisiac, and a destroyer of *rakta-pitta* (bleeding disorders).
As much sugar as has been described is always a remover of burning sensations, a pacifier of *rakta-pitta*, and a dispeller of vomiting, fainting, and thirst. (15)
Phanita (treacle) derived from Madhūka flowers is dry; it increases vāta and pitta, destroys kapha, is sweet in taste and in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and cleanses the bladder. (16)
Equal parts of jaggery and sugar are a purifier and digestive of the bladder, a pacifier of pitta, and a destroyer of raktapitta. // 17 //
Sweet sugar (madhura-śarkarā) indeed destroys hiccup and diarrhea;
it is parching, causes a breaking sensation, and is both astringent and sweet. // 18 //
Praise of Sugarcane and its Varieties:
Sugarcane is aphrodisiac, cooling, and alleviates pitta; it is sweet, nourishing, and increases kapha.
It is unctuous, pleasing to the heart, laxative, highly effective at quelling fatigue, and promotes the purification of the urine.
It promotes the increase of fat,
increases [strength], pacifies the impurities, and provides nourishment for the sense organs; it is beneficial when consumed with teeth.
Having squeezed it directly, one should consume the cane-stalk, which is the essence consisting of nectar. // 19 //
The *kāntāra* variety is red in color and likewise shaped like a bud; the *pauṇḍraka* is known to be white. These three types of sugarcane are the most excellent.
The root portion of the sugarcane (*ikṣu*) is sweet,
and its middle portion is likewise sweet;
however, its top portion is salty and light.
(Ap 41) At the time of eating, a man should consume sugarcane before his meal;
for although it is naturally sweet, it becomes sour when eaten [afterwards].
It provokes the wind humor (vāta). // 21 //
Burning, constipating, and exceedingly heavy, it pacifies wasting diseases;
being astringent, it is capable of producing wind and inducing vomiting,
yet when held for some time after crushing all its roots and tips together, it becomes beneficial.
Therefore, this juice from a mechanical device is burning and not beneficial. // 22 //

If, however, the mechanical juice is drunk at that very moment after crushing the root and the middle part, it will then pacify wind and bile, provide nourishment, and purify the waste and urine. (24)
The qualities of molasses and other such substances:

it subdues bile, removes wind, promotes healing, is pleasing to the heart, and alleviates the three humors; through specific combinations, it particularly removes fever and bestows relief from burning heat.
Old jaggery destroys disorders of feces and urine, generates digestive fire, cures itching and urinary disorders, is unctuous, sweet-tasting, light, removes fatigue, and is wholesome. (25)
It wards off burning heat, removes bile, cuts through thirst, and destroys delusion and fainting;
it dispels wasting and satisfies the senses. Indeed, Siddhakhaṇḍa is always cool and perfectly sweet. (26)
It quenches thirst and delusion, dries the mouth, destroys burning fever, removes the impurities of dyspnea, vomiting, intoxication, and fatigue; it is pleasing to the heart and nourishing.

When semen is depleted, when the digestive fire is impaired, when the vital essence is diminished, and in cases of injury, weakness, or even the incurable disease of *raktapitta*, sugar should always be consumed.
Thus ends the section on sugarcane (*ikṣuvarga*) in the *Āyurvedamahodadhi* composed by Suṣeṇa.
(Ap 42) Now the qualities of liquor are described.

The juice of the jambu fruit is an excellent stimulant, exceedingly sharp and hot, and it increases thirst and nourishment; being very sweet, bitter, pungent, and sour, it is most delicious to the palate. // 1 //
Kāpyopā (*kāpyopama*) breaks down phlegm, increases strength, removes asthma and cough, is aphrodisiac, light, hot, promotes digestion of corrupted matter, and bestows an increase in sleep.

In cases of derangement of pitta, blood, and kapha, as well as in irregular fevers, emaciation, and chronic rhinitis, [this treatment] is drying, purifies the channels of the ears, stimulates the appetite, and dries up disorders such as vāta. // 2 //
When used appropriately and consumed constantly, it destroys phlegm;
it is beneficial for both the emaciated and the obese, and being dry, subtle, and cooling, it purifies the channels.
Taken with curd, it removes wind and phlegm; otherwise, it is like poison. // 3 //
Fresh [milk] produces heaviness and other defects, whereas that which is old is otherwise;
it should not be excessively sharp or mild, nor should it have few ingredients or be turbid.
Now, the qualities of wine (*surā*):
It is heavy, it lubricates the heart, it destroys abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), and swelling;
it subdues wind (*vāta*), and it increases fat, blood, breast milk, urine, and phlegm (*kapha*).
Now, the qualities of Vāruṇī: possessing those qualities, Vāruṇī is pleasing to the heart, light, and sharp; it destroys colic, cough, anorexia, dyspnea, constipation, flatulence, and rhinitis. (6)
It is to be taken when hot, fiery, parched, digestive, and a destroyer of swellings;
now follows [the preparation of] *pathyā*, *bibhītaka*, and *surā*.
A woman should not be excessively light-hearted, just as wine made from vibhītaka fruit is not considered wholesome.
It is not excessively contraindicated in cases of ulcers, anemia, or skin diseases.
Now, regarding *yavasurā*:
*yavasurā* causes constipation, is heavy, dry, and aggravates the three *doṣas*.
Now, the qualities of *ariṣṭa*:
*Ariṣṭa* possesses the qualities of its constituent substances and is superior to all other alcoholic liquors (*madhu*).
It cures disorders of the *grahaṇī*, anemia, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, consumption, grief, abdominal enlargements, and fevers. (9)
Iron destroys abdominal tumors and splenic disorders;
it is astringent, pungent, and increases vāta.
Mārdvīka wine is scraping, pleasing to the heart, not excessively hot, sweet, and laxative. // 10 //

Gauḍa [molasses] slightly increases bile and wind; it destroys jaundice, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, and worms; it facilitates the passage of vision, urine, and feces, and it is nourishing and digestive. (11)
It is very hot, pungent, dry, and sour; it is pleasing to the heart, appetizing, and laxative.
They are digestive stimulants, cooling to the touch, and destroyers of anemia and worms;
among molasses, sugarcane juice, honey, and grape wine, they are lighter in succession as listed. (16)
One should know that fermented preparations made from tubers, roots, fruits, and the like are similar;
*śāṇḍākī* is unfermented, while other types are sour with time, appetizing, and light.
Thus ends the section on intoxicants.
(Ap 44) Now follows the section on sour gruel (*kāñjika*).

Fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) is a laxative, sharp, fragrant, very light, warm in touch yet cooling, dry, a destroyer of fatigue, a remover of exhaustion, clarifying, and a purifier of the bladder.

A decoction enema (āsthāpana) is recommended as a light remedy that pacifies poison and dispels diseases of the respiratory tract; gargling (gaṇḍūṣa), when retained, serves to eliminate various mouth ailments and destroy foul odors.
Fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) is purgative, sharp, hot, generates pitta, yet is cooling to the touch.
It removes fatigue and exhaustion, is appetizing, stimulates digestion, and cleanses the bladder. // 1 //
Thus ends the section on fermented gruel (kāñjika).
// Now begins the section on urine. //
The urine of the camel,
cow, goat, sheep, buffalo, elephant, horse, camel,
and donkey is bilious, dry, sharp, hot, pungent in taste, and has a salty aftertaste.

It quickly overcomes worms, swelling, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, colic, anemia, phlegm, and wind; it also conquers abdominal tumors, anorexia, poison, vitiligo, leprosy, and hemorrhoids. The group of urine from camels, cows, goats, sheep, horses, elephants, buffaloes, and donkeys is hot.

Bitter, sharp, light, hot, salty, and flavorful, it increases bile, is purgative, and is dry; it is pleasing to the heart, appetizing, destroys worms, stimulates the digestive fire, and cures skin diseases and urinary disorders; it conquers abdominal tumors, flatulence, hemorrhoids, colic, wind, phlegm, and poisons, and it destroys swelling, anemia, and abdominal enlargement.
Urine likewise destroys the eighteen types of skin diseases, swelling, jaundice, abdominal enlargements, insanity, and disorders of phlegm; it should be used during the dark fortnight.
This [urine] is parching, and when sour, it is recommended for worms.
Thus ends the section on urine.
(Ap 45) // Now follows the section on grains. //
Unctuous, a subduer of *vāta*, a pacifier of the three *doṣas*, always wholesome for living beings,

and the best among nourishing grains— *ṣaṣṭika* rice removes fatigue and eliminates disorders such as urinary distress (*kṛcchra*). Even more so than white rice, it is highly serviceable and brings about great benefit.
When consumed, it removes phlegm (*śukra*), as well as alleviates dyspnea, fatigue, and dispels disorders such as cough.
Sweet in taste and digestion, it pacifies the provocation of wind and phlegm;
it is wholesome during fever and indigestion, removes all types of poison and [diseases] caused by excessive speed,
and is suitable for children, the elderly, women, the delicate, and those who are very comfortable.
For this king is one to be served, indeed a great Śāli tree, free from stain. // 2 //
Grain that is sown and entirely covered by soil is known as the best; that which is sown but emerges partially covered is to be known as middling.
That is inferior, as it bestows the fault of being devoid of essence.
The rice that was burnt, that which was to be ground, and that which was sown in the forest— {cf. Rājanighaṇṭu 16.158ab}.
These indeed have their existence severed; they truly bring about the binding of feces and urine. // 3 //
Rice varieties grown in various regions come in many colors; among them,
this one is naturally preeminent as the supreme pacifier of the three *doṣas*.
Rakta, Bhīrukapuṇḍarīka, Kalamas, Tūrṇa, Mahāpuṣpaka, Dīrgha, Kāñcanahāyana, Asitaśrita, Puṣpapāṇḍaja, and Pāṇḍuka.
The varieties known as Sāgara, Tapanīyaka, Śakunaka, Rodhra, and Saugandhika, along with Dhānā and others, together with Pataṅgin and Dūṣaka, are delightful and auspicious Śāli rice grains.
They are conducive to good digestion, stimulate the appetite, provide strength, are unctuous, alleviate the three *doṣas*,
increase semen and phlegm, improve the relish for food, promote digestion, and are nourishing. (Ap 46)
Beneficial in all diseases, they remove fatigue and destroy hunger, thirst, exhaustion, and the weariness of travel;
among grains, the *ṣaṣṭika*, *kalama*, red rice, and *mahāśāli* are the best. (6)
Rice of various kinds is pleasing to the eyes, satiating, heart-pleasing, digestive for those with weak digestion, heavy, nourishing, and wholesome. // 7 //
It is wakeful, pleasant to the heart, sweet, life-sustaining,
light, aphrodisiac, strength-giving, and when taken with ghee, it destroys the three impurities.
Rice for kings destroys phlegm and wind, is sweet, and wards off bile;
it bestows beauty, semen, great luster, purity of mind, and strength. (9)
Kṛṣṭiśāli destroys the three doṣas, is sweet, and likewise removes emaciation;
it subdues pitta, is slimy, and bestows semen, complexion, beauty, and strength. // 10 //
These qualities of rice have been declared and should be understood by those learned in the scriptures;
furthermore, all forest grasses destroy the disease of leprosy. // 11 //

It quickly removes all diseases and cleanses the mouth. Among grains, *ṣaṣṭika* rice is the best; among meats, goat and partridge meat are beneficial. For drinking water, that which is like black clay is recommended; among milk, clarified butter, and the like, that derived from a cow is praised first.
Thus ends the section on rice.
They are hot, dry, and predominantly astringent-sweet; they are light in digestion,
destroy phlegm (*śleṣman*), generate wind (*pavana*) and bile (*pitta*), and are always constipating.
This description of grains, beginning with *romākā*, has been correctly proclaimed for the benefit of men; thereafter, the sequence is established by means of *bala*, *śāka*, *sadrava*, and *gul*.
Thus ends the section on grains (*dhānyavarga*).
(Ap 47) Now, the qualities of pulse crops are described.
First, the qualities of mung beans (*mudga*):
*Mudga* removes bile and phlegm, heals wounds, destroys diseases of the throat and phlegm, and is light.
It is wholesome for those suffering from wind-diseases and diarrhea, as well as for eye ailments at all times.
It does not cause flatulence, pacifies the wind, and is recommended for those with weak digestion.
