It is the best among soups, improves the voice, and cures urinary disorders.
Now, regarding the mung bean (*māṣa*):
the mung bean is unctuous, a builder of strength and marrow, drying, and increases phlegm; it is hot in potency and quickly provokes blood-bile (*raktapitta*).
When being eaten, it destroys wind, is heavy, possesses an excellent taste, is appetizing, delicious, and is always life-sustaining for men who enjoy physical exertion and comfort. // 1 //
The black gram (*māṣa*) is heavy, causes loose stools and urine, is unctuous, hot in potency, sweet, and subdues *vāyu*. It is nourishing,
specifically increases breast milk, bestows strength, and brings about semen and *kapha*.
Due to the state of being astringent, it does not cause the breaking of feces, nor does it increase urine, nor does it produce phlegm.
Sweet in digestion, sweet, very dense, nourishing, and providing breast milk and relish;
they say the fruit of *ātmaguptā* is equal to black gram (*māṣa*), and the fruit of *kākāṇḍa* is likewise.
Thus ends the qualities of black gram.
(Āyurvedadīpikā 48) Now, the qualities of *kulattha*: black *kulattha* is astringent in taste.
It is pungent in its post-digestive effect and destroys phlegm and wind.
Śrutā (or Śukrā) destroys urinary calculi and tumors, is astringent, and cures chronic catarrh and cough. // 1 //
It cures abdominal tumors, urinary calculi, piles, hiccup, and asthma; it treats blood-bile disorders and destroys phlegm.
It specifically cures eye diseases when combined with wild *kulattha* (horse gram). // 2 //
Now, the properties of rājamāṣa:
rājamāṣa is palatable, increases kapha and semen, and produces acidity and pitta.
It is sweet-tasting, wind-increasing, dry, astringent, and very heavy. // 3 //
The *śimbi* pulse is parching and astringent; it causes the decrease or increase of poison, grief, semen, strength, and vision.
It is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), sweet, and increases feces, urine, wind (*vāta*), and bile (*pitta*).
The *śibis* (or *śimbis*) indeed become of various kinds, with white, black, yellow, and red colors.
Now, the qualities of sesame:
it is slightly astringent, sweet, and bitter;
it is constipating, increases bile, and is likewise hot.
Sesame is sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), most strengthening, unctuous, and is said to be wholesome as an ointment for wounds.
Black sesame is beneficial for the teeth, generates fire and intelligence, produces little urine, promotes breast milk, nourishes the hair, subdues wind, and is heavy.
Among all types of sesame, black is the most excellent; white is purifying, while the others are inferior.

Dantī generates the strength of the teeth, digestive fire, and intellect; it is galactagogue, subdues Vāta, is heavy, unctuous, increases Pitta, and produces scant urine. It is beneficial for the hair, excellent for wounds, astringent, hot, provides stability, and is sweet, bitter, and pungent in its post-digestive transformation (vipāka).
Black sesame is most wholesome, dark sesame is beneficial in small amounts, and other varieties are inferior in quality. (1)
Thus ends the section on sesame seeds.
Now, the qualities of barley gruel (yavāgu) are described.

Barley is astringent and sweet, cooling, and pungent in its post-digestive effect; it subdues phlegm and bile, is always beneficial for wounds like sesame, promotes frequent urination, and cures excessive wind and diarrhea. (1)

It produces stability, digestive fire, the bodily elements (dhātus), and excellence of voice and complexion; it is slightly slimy, acts as a thick scraping agent, removes fat, wind, and thirst, is parching, and clarifies both blood and bile. // 2 //
One should know that anything lacking these qualities is always unlike barley; otherwise, it is not barley at all.
Barley is astringent, sweet, and cold; it is beneficial for urinary disorders and destroys diseases of bile and phlegm.
It promotes the easy passage of feces, is beneficial for the eyes, increases strength, acts as a tonic, is aphrodisiac, and is wholesome for the bodily humors. // 3 //

Veṇuyava is declared to be cooling, astringent, delicious in taste, dry, and a destroyer of urinary disorders, worms, phlegm, and poisons; it is likewise sweet, strengthening, and a remover of pitta. // 4 //
Thus ends the section on bamboo seeds.
Now, the qualities of wheat (*godhūma*):

Wheat is said to be sweet, heavy, strengthening, stabilizing, and a provider of semen and appetite; it is unctuous, extremely cold, a remover of wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*), promotes healing, removes urinary stones, and is laxative. (1)

It is unctuous, sweet in taste, and sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka); it generally resides in the stomach (āmāśaya), is strengthening, cooling, laxative, appetizing, and promotes healing. It is heavy, increases semen and phlegm (kapha), provides stability, and destroys pitta and vāta.
Wheat, however, is captivating, stabilizing, white, and a remover of disorders. (2)
Now, the qualities of *kusumbha*:
*Kusumbha* is pungent, pungent in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), destroys *kapha*, causes a burning sensation, and alleviates *vāta*.

(Āyurveda-prakāśa 51) Now, the qualities of *siddhārtha* (white mustard): it is hot, sweet in taste, subdues wind (*vāta*), increases bile (*pitta*), and is pungent in its post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*).
Siddhārthaka is declared to be pungent both in its post-digestive effect and its taste; it provokes blood and bile. // 1 //
Sharp and hot in potency, it destroys phlegm and wind; likewise, black mustard possesses these same qualities.
Now, the properties of *āḍhakī* (pigeon pea):
they pacify phlegm and wind, and are hot in potency.
They alleviate pain in the heart, back, abdomen, wind (vāta), and bile (pitta), as well as pain in the thighs;

they remove cough, dyspnea, vomiting, thirst, and fever. They are wholesome for itching and skin diseases, and for scabies, leprosy, and fistula-in-ano. Furthermore, *pathyā* (harītakī) is exceedingly beneficial when taken with relish. // 1 //
Āḍhakī destroys phlegm and wind, though it slightly provokes wind.
This food of his is sweet, causes constipation, and is heavy;
it stimulates the digestive fire, subdues kapha and pitta, and destroys all types of urinary disorders (prameha). // 3 //
Having given heart-pleasing and comfortable food, *āḍhakī* and *buddhapūṣaka* are beneficial;
likewise is *sūrīcaikaḍhana*.
The qualities of *mudga* soup are as follows.
The skilled prepare this highly praised mung bean soup, which is rich in the power to remove fever and destroys blood-bile (raktapitta);
when prepared with the addition of fats, it also subdues the wind (vāyu).
It pacifies internal burning and is recommended for all diseases. // 1 //

Light green-gram soup pacifies the excessive fever of bile, removes burning heat, and destroys loss of appetite; if this is combined with rock salt, it clarifies the blood and becomes a remover of all diseases. (Ap 52) // 2 //

Those living beings whose impurities and faults have been removed, whose bodily humors are diminished yet who suffer from excessive thirst, those who are tormented by the Dharma, those consumed by the fire of their mouths, and furthermore those humans overcome by dysentery—they are fit for this mild broth. (3)
The qualities of kulittha-pūṣa (soup).

The *ulā* and *kulittha* pulses of the Vīrya region alleviate phlegm and wind but increase bile and blood; they are sour in their post-digestive effect (*pāka*), and they cure asthma, cough, abdominal enlargement, and pains in the heart, head, and bladder. They are powerful suppressors of urinary obstruction, urinary disorders, and stones, and they cause the cessation of semen.
It is the best [remedy] for diseases such as durnāman (scrofula), kuṣṭha (skin diseases), swelling, disorders of the liver and spleen, gulma (abdominal tumors), and tūnī (colic). // 1 //
The qualities of lentil soup (masūrapūpa).
Māṣūra beans are light, extremely dry and clear, beneficial for the eyes, and they diminish urine, eliminate phlegm, increase bile, improve the appetite, and cause disorders of wind (vāta).
They produce constipation and blockage of the digestive tract, yet they break up stones and relieve difficult urination.
All varieties of māṣa pulse are prescribed for disorders arising from pitta and are pleasing to the heart. // 1 //
(Ap 53) Now, the qualities of the *kalāya* [bean]:
it is wholesome when fresh (*prasūta*).
How does it act?
It is extremely parching, subdues phlegm, and excessively removes bile.
It provides relish, causes colic for men, and is said to be associated with undigested matter (āmānubandhin); such is Kalāpa. // 1 //
Now, the qualities of chickpeas are being described.
They are dry, increase wind (vāta), pacify urinary disorders (prameha), and break up gravel and stones; they cause the loosening of feces, pacify bile (pitta), and produce flatulence;
they remove throat ailments, provide pleasure through good eating, and eliminate loss of appetite.
Split chickpeas are strengthening and complexion-enhancing, yet they are not beneficial for men. // 1 //
Thus ends [the section on] parched chickpeas.
Ārdrā is most aphrodisiac, strengthening, increases phlegm (śleṣman), and promotes appetite;
it pacifies wind (vāta) and bile (pitta), is cooling, and cures dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra). // 2 //
Thus are the fresh chickpeas.
Roasted chickpeas (bhṛṣṭacaṇaka) are light, they alleviate phlegm and fatigue; they cure vomiting, improve the appetite, and provide sleep, comfort, nourishment, and strength. // 3 //
Thus ends [the section on] roasted chickpeas.
A soup made from soaked chickpeas brings about the destruction of burning sensations and eliminates all urinary disorders, even those caused by powerful malevolent forces.
Boiled with Vidala and water, combined with ginger and black pepper, it removes wind diseases and destroys all the humors. // 4 //
Thus ends [the section on] black chickpeas.

White chickpeas (*caṇaka*) alleviate bile (*pitta*), yet they provoke phlegm (*śleṣman*) and wind (*vāta*); they provide strength, cause the retention of waste, and are associated with weak digestion. // 5 //
The water from the Caṇa plant, cool as moonbeams, removes the ailments of urinary disorders, bile, and blood.
The oil (itself) is indeed nourishing in its digestive transformation; it is satiating and possesses a sweetness that is pleasing to virtuous people. // 6 //
Thus concludes the section on white chickpeas.
Śyāmāka, kodrava, and whatever other pulses (śimbika) there may be—these are unwholesome; they do not recommend them for those who are healthy and free from disease. // 1 //
Whatever decays very quickly is considered to be lighter;
barley, wheat, beans, and even fresh sesame seeds are beneficial. (2)
Thus ends the section on grains.
May there be well-being for both the scribe and the reciter.
Salutations to the illustrious Sāmbasadāśiva.
May there be prosperity!
(Ap 55) Now, the qualities of cooked food.
The wheat *pheṇikā*—light, beautiful, and desirable—is highly praised; it strengthens the body, is easily digested, and destroys vomiting.
It turns back the mouth of the *badala* [disease] and [removes] half-[the affliction].
In cases of bilious vomiting (āmlopavāsa), it relieves the burning sensation when combined with wheat and prepared as a suitable food for filling the stomach. // 1 //
Pheṇiyā.
Preparations made from the flour of black gram (māṣa) are nourishing, unctuous, strengthening, and highly productive of semen; they bestow great exhilaration upon women. // 2 //
They say that wheat is sāṃjila.

Having thoroughly kneaded it with curd and clarified butter, and having made it equal in measure with sugar, one should cook it in well-heated jaggery and clarified butter; then, once it has become soft like fire, one should bind it securely, adding camphor, black pepper, rock salt, and the four aromatic spices (caturjātaka).
The sages call this great modaka by the name Puṣpālamba. // 3 //
These aphrodisiacs, which arouse passion like fire when properly nourished, bestow pleasure and relish;
when eaten, these delightful sweetmeats dispel wind and bile, bringing joy to men.
The *modaka* is exceedingly aphrodisiac, increases *śleṣman*, and due to its long digestion,
it likewise weakens the digestive fire and causes heaviness of the abdomen.
The modaka always bestows superior strength. // 5 //
The fruit of immortality.

It pacifies excessive bile, alleviates the provocation of phlegm, generates digestive fire, and destroys diseases of wind. Physicians praise the noble and beautiful *amṛtaphala* as that which instantly removes the exhaustion born of sexual pleasure; they declare it excellent. (6)
It pacifies hemorrhoids and dysuria, and likewise removes wind and bile.
A trail of camphor.
It is pleasing, strengthening, a promoter of strength and luster, and possesses a heart-pleasing fragrance; it stabilizes the body, produces brilliance and complexion,
increases semen, generates an abundance of fat, and is highly recommended for bile disorders.
It is cooked in ghee and combined with aguru, honey, and elā.
This [substance], beginning with camphor, which causes the breaking [of ailments], destroys pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman),
and is most beneficial for the world, should be eaten as a tonic (tālaka-dinī).
Clarified butter, parched grain flour, cakes, small balls, large balls, and so forth, are aphrodisiacs, appetizers, strengthening, and heavy, according to their respective natures. (9)
Indrārikā.
Indrārikā.
It is aphrodisiac, appetizing, digestive-stimulant, strengthening, heavy, and causes secretions;
it provides nourishment for the vital breaths, is flavorful, and increases phlegm. It pacifies abdominal distension, constipation, and abdominal tumors, and it cuts through bile and blood disorders.
And she who is constantly filled with affection is Indrārikā, who is to be consumed as food.
Filled with fortitude.
Dhṛtapūra is strengthening, aphrodisiac, sweet, and cooling;
it subdues vāta and raktapitta, and especially increases kapha.
Sāḍiyā (Bhāṣya)
Kṣārakharjūrikā is unctuous and bestows semen, flesh, and strength;
it is strengthening, aphrodisiac, pleasing to the heart, and destroys vomiting and loss of appetite.
The Milk Grove.
This very smooth pill, when softened with milk, bestows luster and happiness;
it generates strength against thirst, pacifies fatigue, and is difficult to digest for those with weak digestion.
It constantly destroys bile and blood; when prepared with ghee and eaten, this pill is said to provide excellent nourishment and kindle the fire of desire. (13)
A milk-ball (kṣīra-vaṭikā) cooked in oil.
Very smooth milk-vatukas bestow luster, happiness, and strength;
those vatukas made from meat and cooked in oil subdue the wind disorder (vāta). 14.
(Mudgavaṭakas:
Whatever light and appetizing foods are derived from mung beans, these are called *mudgavaṭakas*. (Bhā.)
Those prepared from chickpeas and similar legumes are considered difficult to digest, light, and dry. // 15 //
Kāñjīka-vaṭakas (balls made from sour gruel).
Meat-based vaṭakas (meatballs) placed in sour gruel (kāñjika) destroy wind (vāta), stimulate the appetite, are pleasing to the heart, and aggravate phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta). // 16 //
Processed with the powder of *rājikā* (black mustard),

or mixed with the powder of *rājī*, it removes phlegm and wind, acts as an appetizer and digestive stimulant, destroys weak digestion, pacifies impurities and poisons, and ensures the digestion of all food.
Or else, when mixed with water and combined with jaggery and salt, it destroys bile, blood disorders, and the like;
it removes thirst, fainting, blows, fever, and wind-disorders, and it is a destroyer of minor diseases. // 17 //
Buttermilk combined with tender ginger-sprouts and *kustumburī*,
properly stirred until half-dried, should be placed in another vessel covered with fine incense; from this,
delightful buttermilk-balls (*vaṭaka*) are produced, which possess both flavor and softness.
The earth knows those [fruits] which daily bear a flavor possessing a fragrance like that of wine;
this is the sour *vaṭaka* (sour tamarind).
A well-cooked dish filled with cumin, *bāhlīka*, ginger, black pepper, and rock salt is most delicious when prepared with curd, *mathita* yogurt, and *tālī*. (Ap 59)
Having been prepared with kṛtāñjali, boiled, stirred, and left to rest at will, this sour meat-balls (*amlavaṭaka*) directly destroys even the most loathsome diseases. (19)
Various types of *vaṭaka* (balls):
*Vaṭakas* and *vaṭikās* are prepared from ground half-pumpkin, long pepper, rock salt, and *methikā*, combined with the flour of split black gram (*māṣa*). // 20 //
Cakes made of kōhalā (Bhāṣya)
Wheat cakes.
Smooth wheat flour, its surface covered with reeds and sprinkled with sweet water,
is kneaded by beautiful women and rolled into balls;
these are then placed in a vessel heated within, and with hands joined together, long white *maṇḍakas* are fashioned from the finely ground powder.
Placed in vessels, they become perfectly prepared, bubbling and swelling as they cook. // 21 //

These foods, prepared with appropriate methods of cooking, should be eaten together with attendants, mixed with mung-bean broth, or with *āḍhakī* or lentil soups, along with the juices of meat from wild or marshy animals seasoned with ghee.
This meal, taken at the proper time— at the beginning of the second watch during the spring and other seasons— is a constant and wholesome regimen.
In the summer season, the king's food should consist of milk and clarified butter mixed with water. // 22 //
Wheat cakes are appetizing, light, warming, and digestive; they are especially beneficial when consumed with whey.
Maṇḍakas and maṇḍikās, as well as pathyās roasted on coals, [are beneficial]. // 23 //
Mandakas that are too hot are wholesome, while those that are excessively cold are considered heavy.
[One should avoid] those cooked in a pit of hot ashes, in a potsherd, on a frying pan, in a vessel, or over glowing embers. (Ap 60.24)
One should know that blue and yellow [cakes] are progressively [superior];
[the latter] destroys blood [disorders], provokes *pitta*, is sweet, and subdues *vāta*.
Wheat baked on charcoal is aphrodisiac, digestive, and an aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*). (26)
Now, the qualities of foods such as *vaṭaka* (meatballs) and others.
Filled to the brim with Bāhlīja, Mārica, and abundant Lavaṇapṛthu and Ārdraka, it is steamed until savory, fragrant, rich in aroma, tender, and the color of saffron.
When dropped between his teeth, he makes a distinct "murmur-murmur" sound; or rather, how fortunate is he when a ball, affectionately given by his beloved, enters his cheek! (27)
Koravaḍā (Bhā.)
Curd-filled dumplings.
Vatukas made from curd itself, combined with rice flour, sugar, and curd, are proclaimed to pacify severe wind disorders, provide relish, and even remove formidable bile. (28)
Those made from chickpeas (*caṇaka*) and similar ingredients are difficult to digest and cause a significant impairment of the digestive fire (*vahnimāndya*).
One should provide fillings such as black gram (*māṣa*) and the like, which are light, appetizing, and stimulate the digestive fire. (29)
That which is sweet or sweet-sour produces those very same effects and generates an aggravation of phlegm; this is known as *cāṇakya-pūraṇa*.
Veṅgaṇī (Bhāṣya)
They call "veṣṭanikā" well-cooked flour made from mung and black gram beans wrapped in a mass of wheat flour;
by eating it, one obtains (or enjoys) great power.
A human being [should be anointed] with oil, or with ghee, or with something fragrant. // 31 //
In this world, the group of edible foods is both relished and prepared as long as they are cooked over glowing coals and bathed in very hot ghee. (32)
The consumption of food prepared with oil and mixed with jaggery and wheat produces phlegm and bile, and it subdues the wind (vāta). //33//
[The bhāvanā] on the simile of the oil lamp.
Those derived from *śāli* rice are light, easily digestible, palatable, and subdue *kapha*;
those derived from *śāli*, mung beans, and other such grains are heavy and appetizing.
Rice, mung beans, and parched grain (in measure).
Pāyasa (milk-rice) is constipating, strengthening, increases fat and phlegm, and is heavy;
kṛśarā (rice and pulse porridge) generates phlegm and bile, is strengthening, and destroys wind.
Pills cooked in oil with rice, as well as indigestible roasted grains and the consumption of *rocana*, immediately provoke an excess of phlegm; this is especially true for crumbled *kūravaḍas*. (36)
Kūravaḍas (Bhāṣya)
Barley flour (saktu) is nourishing, aphrodisiac, and removes thirst, pitta, and kapha; it is appetizing, provides immediate strength, is laxative, and alleviates vāta. (37)
But she (is) [to be] brought forth.
Food made from flour that has been kneaded together causes worms;
however, that which is produced from rice is very difficult to digest, possesses a sweet taste, and is nourishing.
Rice-pounding board (box) //
Thus ends the section on prepared foods in the Great Ocean of Ayurveda composed by Suṣeṇa.
Now, the qualities of the fruits are described.
First, therein, are the qualities of the pomegranate.
It pacifies the three doṣas, is wholesome, aphrodisiac, sweet, and cooling; it destroys vomiting, anorexia, and thirst, and removes swelling and pitta-fever. // 1 //
When sprinkled with water after being heated,
it pacifies bile and destroys all diseases.
A well-ripened pomegranate fruit is pleasing to the heart and promotes strength and complexion.
It is declared by the learned to be extremely sour and sweet, possessing an astringent quality; in its taste and potency, it is pacifying, subdues wind, removes bile, and stimulates digestion;
it is slightly astringent and generally dispels phlegm, yet in its post-digestive state (pāka), it is again... [sweet].
Thus, the pomegranate is renowned for its excellence in taste, potency, post-digestive transformation, and its various qualities. // 3 //
Pomegranate is of two kinds, praised by those who have wives: one is sour and the other is sweet.
Among them, the sour variety removes wind and phlegm, while the sweet variety removes heat, is light, and is wholesome. (4)
Pomegranate is sweet, sour, and astringent; it destroys cough, wind, phlegm, and bile.
It is constipating, stimulates digestion, is light and hot, cooling, removes vertigo, and provides appetite. (5)
Thus [ends the section on] the pomegranate.
Now, the qualities of grapes.

Grape is beneficial for the eyes, pacifies *rakta-pitta*, is sweet, cold in potency, sweet in its post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*), unctuous, slightly astringent, heavy, and a remover of the defects of thirst and emaciation.
It is [beneficial] for those with wasting (*kṣīṇa*).
It removes vomiting, dyspnea, cough, and the pain of fever;
it cures bitterness of the mouth and intoxication. Among the most excellent fruits, it is declared to be the best. (6)
Well-cooked.
Grapes indeed increase the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), are nourishing, eliminate the *doṣas*,
alleviate thirst and fatigue, pacify *vāta*, and destroy the disease of vomiting;
they are sour in digestion, pleasant in aroma, sweet in taste, and cooling.
That [potion], when prepared with vigor, becomes pacifying and, once matured, serves to purify the feces and urine in cases of fever caused by phlegm.
Cold and sour [substances] pacify the disorder of wind; sweet substances, being pleasant in taste and digestion, are appetizing.
It is beneficial for the eyes and pacifies asthma, cough, fatigue, and vomiting; it destroys consumption, thirst, and fever.
The parched and dried grape, when highly nourishing, removes burning sensations, flatulence, fatigue, and other ailments;
while the jujube fruit (kola), though its potency may have diminished, makes even those who are extremely debilitated capable of sexual pleasure. // 8 //
Thus ends the section on grapes.
Now, the qualities of the mātuliṅga.
The *cakra* (skin) is bitter and pungent; it destroys *kapha* and worms, is unctuous, and subdues *vāta*.

Flesh is nourishing, pacifies *vāta* and *pitta*, is aphrodisiac, and is very difficult to digest. The *kesara* (filaments) are sour, generate an increase in digestive fire (*agni*), and alleviate *śvāsa* and *kāsa*.
That which arises from the mātuliṅga fruit removes hiccup, vomiting, thirst, and numbness of the mouth. // 1 //
The rind of the mātuliṅga is bitter and unctuous,
while its pulp is pungent, unctuous, sweet, nourishing, and [remedial] for vāta and pitta.
Flesh that is broken down becomes unctuous and light; its filaments cure cough, hiccup, asthma, phlegm, wind, and abdominal diseases, as well as gulma, colic, and disorders of the wind. // 10 //
In the Sindhu region during the autumn season, when the clouds have gathered and it is clothed in mist;

O King, physicians prescribe *sālu* (mātu) prepared with salt, fresh asafoetida, and black pepper, combined with powdered white mustard in the winter; likewise in the cool season and spring, and in the summer, it is to be taken combined with jaggery.
The *liṅga* has been described as common to all seasons. // 11 //
Now, the citron.
The jambīra is sour in taste and in its post-digestive effect; it subdues vāta while increasing pitta and kapha.
It quickly stimulates the appetite and increases the digestive fire, acting as a digestive aid for food. (12)
Pungent, sweet, and sour—well-known among tastes, it is appetizing, stimulates the digestive fire, and subdues wind. It destroys... [the humors].
Kapha and wind strike at the potency of pitta, which is the fruit of its action; thus is this vāta-pitta fully ripened. // 13 //
Even its preparation is not pleasing, yet it causes the aggravation of *raktapitta*.
The lime fruit (*nimbūphala*) is appetizing, increases the digestive fire, and aggravates *pitta* along with *vāta* and blood.
It impairs vision, specifically produces *śleṣman*, and brings about the immediate digestion of consumed food and drink. (14)
The lime (nimbuka) is known to destroy swarms of worms; it is sharp and sour, and is said to cure abdominal ailments.
It is beneficial for wind, bile, phlegm, and colic, and it restores appetite for lost grains while providing digestive power. 15.
Now, the orange fruit.

The fruit of the orange provides strength; it is delicious, pleasing to the heart, light, excellent, kindling of the digestive fire, a pacifier of burning sensations, and a promoter of the digestion of consumed food.
It destroys all forms of anorexia, removes fatigue, dispels wind disorders, and bestows nourishment.
Even after eating it, when consumed as a secondary medicine, it does not produce any adverse effect in humans. // 16 //

The noble-minded lords of sages declare that the orange fruit is slightly sour, sweet, and cool; it is pungent and bitter due to its potency, and through its digestion, it pacifies, stimulates the digestive fire, and ripens undigested matter; it alleviates wind, removes phlegm and bile, and is so in its post-digestive state. (17)
Now, the honey-cucumber.

Physicians always declare that madhukarkaṭī is delicious in its cooked state and in its natural flavor; it dissolves the provocation of blood and bile (raktapitta) when they are sluggish and constantly destroys burning fever. 18.
Now, the mocā fruit.
Moca fruit is sweet in taste, sweet in post-digestive effect (vipāka), cold in potency (vīrya),
heavy, dull, pacifies pitta, removes vāta, and is beneficial when the digestive fire is weak;
it increases the quantity of food recently eaten, removes fatigue, allays thirst, and bestows tranquility.
It provides comfort to those with a blazing digestive fire, removes diseases caused by phlegm, and brings nourishment to living beings. // 19 //
Now, the coconut fruit.
It is unctuous, sweet in taste, sweet in post-digestive effect (vipāka), pleasing to the heart, difficult to digest when old,
subdues pitta, increases worms, causes intoxication, destroys diseases of vāta,
aggravates undigested matter (āma) and kapha, pacifies the digestive fire, and dispels vertigo.
The coconut fruit and coconut water greatly increase the strength of Kandarpa.
The water of the coconut is delicious, aphrodisiac, light, digestive-stimulant, dry, and cold; it alleviates wind and bile and is a cause for purification of the bladder.
Physicians say that this moon-like water is wholesome for bile-fever and a destroyer of poisons. (20)
(Āp 66) Now, the fruit of the possible.
It is wholesome, highly nutritious, sweet with a slight sourness, and appetizing; it subdues wind, removes unpleasant tastes, and stimulates the digestive fire. // 21 //
Now, the fruit of the *āmalakī* tree.

The *karamara* fruit (*dhātrī*) destroys wind (*vāta*) because of its acidity; it subdues wind and bile (*pitta*) because of its sweetness and coolness; and it conquers phlegm (*kapha*) because of its dryness and astringency; thus, the fruit of the *dhātrī* overcomes all three *doṣas*. (22)
... likewise. (cf. Bhāvamiśra: Bhāvaprakāśaḥ 41)

The dhātrī fruit is slightly sweet in taste, sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and it destroys the three doṣas; it removes urinary disorders, pacifies prameha, and eliminates constipation; it is beneficial whether eaten before or after a meal, possesses the essence of nectar, and is always wholesome. (23)

It is dry, sweet, astringent, sour, and pungent; it is unctuous, highly appetizing, beneficial for the eyes, bestowing strength and complexion, providing fortitude, aphrodisiac, and granting intelligence.
It destroys itching and skin diseases, removes fever, and wards off thirst, burning sensations, and heat.
In short, the fruit of the dhātrī tree, once produced, pacifies the three humors for all living beings. // 24 //
The three types of *dhātrī* fruit (the *āmalaka*) destroy urinary disorders (*meha*), loss of appetite, and various other ailments when consumed daily.
And sourness, by virtue of its sweetness and astringency, respectively destroys the three doshas; it is light and possesses a cold potency. // 25 //
The fruit of the *prācīnāmalaka* tree.
Prācīnāmalaka is aphrodisiac, sweet, pleasing to the heart, and alleviates *kapha*;
it is cooling and an aphrodisiac.
It promotes longevity and is the supreme remedy for fever with a burning sensation. // 26 //
(Āp 67) Now, the mango fruit.

The immature [milk] generates wind, bile, phlegm, and blood; when it has become thick and similarly ripened, it possesses a sweet taste, pacifies the three humors, and bestows nourishment upon the emaciated limbs.

Among fruits, the āmla (tamarind) is the best; it increases the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), has a sweet post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), is nourishing, bestows luster, wards off thirst and emaciation, and stimulates the appetite. (27)
The mango tree itself is the sovereign of fruits; it nourishes all the sense organs, bestows strength, is most aphrodisiac, and is pleasing to the heart; it grants immense delight among women. (28)

At the time of its ripening, the mango is sweet in taste with a slight acidity; it is pleasing to the heart, promotes the increase of semen, pacifies the wind (vāta), and acts as a digestive and appetizer.
It bestows bliss and imparts strength through virility—so say Suśruta and others.
For they are renowned throughout the entire world as producing an excess of phlegm and being difficult to digest. // 29 //
That which is known by the distinguished Buddhas as the "Lip-sucker of the Lustful One," and which was drawn from the ocean by the gods led by the Daityas with great effort;

That which appears falsely according to various tastes and in accordance with one's own nature— that very thing was created by the Lord through his creative power as nectar, consisting of the essence of flavor, which removes all doubt.
Now, the wood-apple fruit.
Raw wood-apple is harmful to the throat and excessively causes numbness of the tongue; it aggravates the three humors (doṣas), yet it is an antidote to poison, astringent, and appetizing.
When ripe, it is capable of dispelling asthma, vomiting, fatigue, exhaustion, thirst, and hiccups.
It is said that everything which is astringent and removes poison should therefore always be used.
Phaṇāsa (bhā-) //
It is difficult to digest, sweet and sour, and it destroys wind and bile;
it pacifies wind and bile, is heavy, and causes the digestive fire to become dull. // 32 //
The bark is sweet, nourishing, aphrodisiac, and increases bile;
they say that the fruit-stalk (mañji) is the best in quality, as it subdues bile, is sweet, and is pleasing to the heart. (33)
It is astringent-sweet, parching, pungent, and increases phlegm; it is constipating, difficult to digest, acts upon the tip of the tongue, is dull, and heavy. (34)
Ṭeṃbaru (Bhāṣā)
Now, the qualities of *karamarda*.
The karamarda fruit is very sweet when well-ripened, yet possesses a sour taste;
it pacifies wind and bile and destroys phlegm and worms. // 65 //
This is to be done by hand. (Bhāṣya)
Now, the qualities of the tamarind (ciñcā).
The ripe fruit of *amlikā* is highly provocative of blood and bile (*raktapitta*).
Its bark-ash is astringent and hot; it destroys *kapha*, parasites, and wind (*anila*). (36)
Tamarind.
Now, the qualities of *bhallātaka*.
The bark and pulp of bhallātaka are nourishing, sweet, and cooling;
its seeds are like fire, promote intelligence, and are excellent for alleviating kapha and vāta. (37)
Bimbadām (to shine)
(Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 6.9) Now, the date-palm.

The date palm fruit pacifies *rakta-pitta* (bleeding disorders), being sweet in taste and sweet in post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and exceedingly cold in potency; it removes thirst and emaciation, and dispels poison, intoxication, diseases, dyspnea, and hiccups.
It is unctuous, aphrodisiac, generates excessive phlegm (*kapha*), and causes a marked dulling of the digestive fire (*agni*).
Indeed, through the application of nourishment, it bestows beauty upon the body and excessively destroys dysuria. // 38 //
The pulp of the date fruit is said to have exactly the same properties;
it is especially recommended for upward-moving blood, burning sensations, and bile disorders. (39)
Now, the sindīphala.
Sindola pacifies kapha, vāta, and pitta; it cures bloody diarrhea, ringworm, leprosy, fistula-in-ano, and scabies, and it breaks even severe urinary stones.
The fruit of the *sindī* tree is always beneficial for heart diseases, provides strength, kindles the fire of desire, and is recommended for cough, emaciation, purgation, and fever. (40)
Now, the golden plantain fruit.
Suvarṇamocā removes phlegm, bile, and wind; it causes constipation and acts as a digestive stimulant.
It is difficult to digest, alleviates burning sensations, and certainly pacifies blood disorders along with bile. (41)
And she shines forth.
Slightly astringent and sweet, it subdues wind and bile; it is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and pleasing to the heart, and it is especially heavy. (49)
(Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 7.10) Now follows the ritual concerning the pippala fruit.
The fruits of the Aśvattha tree are exceedingly wholesome, pleasing to the heart, and very cooling;
they subdue bile along with blood, as well as burning sensations, thirst, vomiting, and loss of appetite. (43)
The fruit of the udumbara tree destroys bile, blood disorders, poison, pain, burning sensations, thirst, vomiting, emaciation, and loss of appetite, and it neutralizes the humors.
The fruit of the udumbara tree is exceedingly cooling and immediately checks even severe blood-bile (rakta-pitta). // 44 //
Now, the umbī fruit.
It causes an extremely severe obstruction of urine, especially that which is associated with blood and wind.
Now, the fruit of the *rājakośātakī*.

Surājakosātaki destroys pitta in major diseases, as well as in consumption, alcoholism, fatigue, exhaustion, urinary disorders, fistula-in-ano, wounds, and various forms of pitta; it is always wholesome [in these conditions]. 45.
Now, the fruit of the *sirākośātakī*.
The Sirākośātakī removes pitta, destroys hunger and thirst, is beneficial in urinary disorders (meha), is hot in potency, and cures vomiting caused by pitta. // 46 //
Thus ends the section on fruits in the Great Ocean of Āyurveda composed by Suṣeṇa.
(Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.5.17) Now follows the section on vegetables.
Fruit, fully ripened vegetables, those that are quickly dried, as well as tender and fresh ones; leaves, flowers, fruit, stalks, bulbs, and likewise those born of moisture. // 1 //
Six kinds of leafy vegetables (śāka) have been specified; one should know them all in ascending order:
*sarvaśāka*, *ajāhṛya*, *abhaka*, *jūṣa*, *apairuṣa*, and [the sixth]. // 2 //
Elsewhere, indeed, there are the *sumadhyastha*, *kālaśāka*, and *punarnavā* [plants].
Now, the properties of *taṇḍulīyaka*.
It is cold, dry, and exceedingly light; it removes bile and blood disorders, being sweet both in its post-digestive effect and in its taste, and is most heart-pleasing.
It destroys diseases born of irregular poisons and pacifies the provocation of phlegm and wind.
Fresh *taṇḍulīya* (rice-plant) is extremely wholesome for the immediate dissolution of phlegm. // 3 //

The *taṇḍulīya* is sweet in taste and post-digestive effect, extremely cold, parching, and cooling; it destroys phlegm (*kapha*) and specifically overcomes burning sensations, bile, blood disorders, and poison.
Alternatively, there is the vāstuka and cillī leaf-vegetable.
The *vāstuka* is a digestive stimulant; it is sweet in taste, removes *pitta*, is beneficial for the eyes, unctuous, destroys *vāta*, kills worms, and eliminates disorders such as *kuṣṭha*.
It purifies the feces and urine, subdues diseases of *śleṣman*, and likewise acts as a general reducer of humors.
Even among vegetables, that which is the best is the lightest and always wholesome for living beings. // 5 //
Among all types of dwelling sites, the Kaṭha-vāstuka is praised; the Cilli should be known as a dwelling site slightly inferior to that. (6)
Sakṣāra (alkaline salt) conquers worms, pacifies the three doṣas, stimulates digestion, promotes digestion, improves vision, is sweet, laxative, relishesome,
removes constipation and colic, purifies feces and urine, improves the voice, is unctuous, and is pungent in its post-digestive effect.
The *vāstuka* plant likewise pacifies all diseases, and the *cillī* is equally excellent.
Cillitākavalā (Bhāṣya)
Now, regarding the śigru vegetable:
It pacifies phlegm and wind, produces heat and kindles the digestive fire; it is pleasing to the heart, destroys worms, promotes appetite, and eliminates flatulence and constipation. (8)
[Śigru-vegetable], and then the royal ones (rājakā).

Mustard destroys phlegm and wind, improves the complexion, stimulates the digestive fire, and is beneficial for the heart; it destroys throat pain and worms, possesses a hot potency, and alleviates colic. (9)
[The syllable] madgarīyā [is the essence of] bhā.
Now follows the Śatapuṣpā.
Śatapuṣpā destroys wind, removes colic, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the abdomen;
it is especially digestive and slightly aggravates bile.
Now, regarding cumin.
Fragrant kustumburī is known to pacify vāta and pitta, is light, appetizing, beneficial in fever, used as a condiment or garnish, cooling, and fresh. (11)
Now follows the Rājavallī.

It is strengthening, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the throat, and it removes phlegm and wind; it is commended in cases of the three *doṣas*, light, and it pacifies urinary retention while inducing vomiting; likewise, it cures dysuria.
It is an antidote to poisons and irregular fevers, digestive, and is the best among leafy vegetables.
The royal creeper (*rājavallī*) causes the increase of the leaves and the growth of the fruits of the *marula* tree. // 12 //
Now, the Kusumbhī.

The safflower vegetable (kausumbha-śāka) is said to be excellent; it specifically bestows clarity of vision, provides relish, and increases the luster of the digestive fire; it removes disorders of feces and urine and destroys impurities. (13)
Now, regarding mustard seed.

This mustard vegetable (sārṣapa-śāka) possesses an excessively hot potency; it causes inflammation of the digestive fire, as well as blood disorders, biliousness, and throat diseases. It impairs vision, produces semen, and is burning to the stomach; therefore, it is certainly not wholesome. 14.
(Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.5.17.23) Now,
as for the eggplant.
// Sadāśiva //
Alkaline, it removes phlegm and bile (and wind), produces waste matter, stimulates the digestive fire,
and is bitter, hot, and sweet; yet, being slightly pungent in taste, it slightly increases bile.

Heart-pleasing and beneficial for wind disorders, yet not wholesome for those who drink alcohol—among all such substances, however, the eggplant (*vārtāka*), when fully developed and full of juice, is beneficial when young and not overripe; it is heart-pleasing, appetizing, non-bile-producing, a subduer of *kapha* and wind, and the best of all vegetables. (15)
The eggplant (vārtāka) destroys phlegm and wind, slightly aggravates bile, is said to be flavorful and diuretic; it is indeed beneficial for strength when young. (16)

This excellent, well-prepared dish, seasoned with salt and black pepper powder, enriched with asafoetida, cooked in the mouth of fire, and finished with jackfruit, is renowned for curing phlegm, subduing the primary wind (vāta), and is fit for filling the stomach. 17.
Then there were eggplants filled with bimbi fruits.
The fruit of the *bimbī* is sweet and cooling; through its astringency, it is a styptic and a drying agent.
It alleviates bile, blood disorders, burning sensations, and swelling, yet it causes wind, flatulence, and constipation. (18)
The fruit of the *bimba* tree.
Now, the pharkoṭī fruit.

Bitter, very sharp, sweet, and likewise sour, it removes wind and destroys bile; it generates phlegm, induces consciousness, stimulates digestion and ripening, and for men, it produces fire like a crore-fold [power]. (19)
The fruit of *karkoṭikā* removes abdominal tumors, colic, pitta, and kapha;
it destroys the three doṣas, urinary disorders, and skin diseases, and is slightly sweet and bitter. (20)
It cures cough, dyspnea, and fever; it is a supreme subduer of wind and is very light.
Kaṅkoḍā-bhā.
Now, the properties of radish.

Slightly alkaline, bitter, and endowed with a pungent taste, it is diuretic, removes the *doṣas*, and is excellent for abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and wasting diseases; it is most powerful in cases of severe dyspnea and cough.
It is beneficial for the throat, excellent for the voice, relieves pain, and cures eye diseases.
It may be that even a large quantity of *bālamūla*, when cooked until tender, is beneficial in cases of wind (*samīra*). (21)
The roots are non-existent.
Now, as for the suraṇa root.
It is palatable, digestive, and carminative; it destroys worms, kindles a sluggish digestive fire, is heart-tonic, increases phlegm, is light, promotes strength, and eradicates hemorrhoids.
It sharpens the senses and removes asthma and cough.
It is beneficial for the eyes, easily digestible, memory-enhancing, and removes pain in the heart and the sides of the chest.
The suraṇa root.
Now, the bhūkanda and the piṇḍālu are [also used].

The *bhūkaṇḍa* (earth-root) is extremely windy, strength-promoting, and excessively increases phlegm; it causes constipation, is heavy, and even though it is fatty, it is irregular and a producer of wind-diseases.
It causes urinary disorders (*meha*) and the pain of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), yet it constantly removes *vātarakta*.
Piṇḍālu removes worms from the digestive tract, relieves dysuria, destroys diseases of bile, and acts as an aphrodisiac.
[This is] Piṇḍālu.
(ĀpDhS 1.7.6) Now, regarding the *ārdraka* [garlic]:

Fresh [milk] is digestive, carminative, appetizing, aphrodisiac, slightly warm, excellent, nourishing for all [the tissues], a remover of diseases caused by *kapha*, a destroyer of swelling, a conqueror of colic,
a cleanser of the tongue and throat, and when salted, it is always wholesome as food.
Ground with lime juice, it removes phlegm, stimulates the digestive fire, and promotes healing. // 24 //
Ginger combined with nimbu and āmudra removes blood-bile (asrapitta);
it should be administered as it stimulates the appetite, is beneficial for the heart, and dispels the three doṣas. (25)
// Ginger //
Now, the qualities of the tubers of the kumuda, utpala, and padma lotuses.
The rhizomes of the kumuda, utpala, and padma are provocative of wind (vāta),
astringent, pacifiers of bile (pitta), sweet in their post-digestive transformation (vipāka), and cooling.

These bulbous roots are pleasing to the heart, alleviate *kapha*, and are pungent; they aggravate *pitta*, cure urinary disorders (*meha*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), and worms, and are aphrodisiac, strengthening, and rejuvenative (*rasāyana*). // 27 //
The bulbs of the kumuda, utpala, and padma are beneficial, cooling, sweet, and astringent; they destroy bile, blood disorders, and burning sensations. (28)
The lotus bulb.
Now, the qualities of lotus stalks.
The lotus stalk is cooling, destroys blood-bile (raktapitta), is highly effective in removing burning sensations and fever, is aphrodisiac, and cures thirst and vomiting. (29)
A lotus stalk.
(Ap 77) Now, the qualities of the *śṛṅgāṭaka* (water chestnut).

Śṛṅgāṭaka removes blood-bile, is light, laxative, and especially highly aphrodisiac; it destroys the three doṣas, the three types of distress, and emaciation, provides relish, and cures burning sensations in the urinary tract. // 30 //
Now, the qualities of vārikaśeruka.

Water from the *kāśeru* plant is sweet and cold; it destroys hemorrhagic disorders (*asrapitta*), loss of appetite, vomiting, delusion, and burning sensations. It removes thirst, intoxication, and fatigue, soothes dryness of the throat and mouth, and is heavy. It is highly beneficial in cases of *raktapitta* and for those who are emaciated. // 31 //
Now follows the enumeration of the bulbous roots to be avoided.
One should avoid a bulb that is immature, past its season, decayed, pierced, or eaten by worms; likewise, one should avoid any bulb that does not grow properly.
Now, the qualities of *kaliṅga*.
Kaliṅga removes all defects, is pleasing to the heart, wholesome for those with seminal disorders, causes the loss of vision and semen, and conquers kapha and vāta. (33)
// Kaliṅga //
Now, the qualities of the kūṣmāṇḍa gourd.
It is aphrodisiac, improves the complexion, generates strength, removes pitta, conquers vāta,
cures urinary retention, pacifies prameha, and excises painful urination and stones.

Physicians declare that the kūṣmāṇḍa is the most excellent among the fruits of the creeper; it alleviates the exhaustion caused by feces and urine, pacifies the affliction of thirst, and bestows nourishment upon emaciated limbs. (34)
It relieves urinary obstruction, promotes copious urination, alleviates painful dysuria and urinary stones, and subdues pitta. It is wholesome for blood disorders and for severe pitta diseases,
removes thirst, and brings equilibrium to the three [humors].
They cite this as an example. // 35 //
Now, the qualities of the urvāruka fruit:

The urvāruka is a pitta-alleviator, very cooling, a destroyer of urinary disorders, and an inducer of appetite; it is well-sweet, pacifies burning sensations, and is recommended in diseases of pitta, with the exception of diseases of kapha. (36)
All varieties of sand are difficult to digest and heavy;
they diminish the digestive fire and cause blood-bile disorders. // 37 //
The sand-pile.
Now, regarding Sindhanī:
Sindhana salt pacifies vāta, is aphrodisiac, sweet, and cooling; it is recommended for internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), burning sensations, and various afflictions caused by pitta. (38)
The Sindhu river flows.
Now, the qualities of *cillī*, *kākamācī*, and so forth.
Ciplī (or llī), like vāstuka, is heart-tonic, astringent, heavy, and increases vāta; kākamācī destroys the three doṣas; and cāṅgerī removes kapha and vāta. // 39 //
Vātahṛt, dīpanī, pañjī, bhāraṅgī, and nālicāṣṭaka are sweet and destroy kapha and pitta; kausumbha removes all diseases. (Ap 79, 40)
Raw radish causes the humors (doṣa), while ripe radish alleviates vāta and kapha.
Black mustard is pitta-increasing, whereas taṇḍulīyaka destroys vāta and kapha.
Carṣābhū destroys vāta and pitta; siddhārtha removes kapha and vāta;
and kāsamardaka destroys worms, pitta, and kapha, while acting as a digestive stimulant (dīpana). // 42 //
Karkoṭaka, along with vārtāka, paṭola, and kāravellaka,
removes the eight types of skin diseases, urinary disorders, fever, dyspnea, cough, fat, and phlegm. (43)
Kūṣmāṇḍa should be known as removing all defects and cleansing the bladder;
the fruits of rājakośātakī and tumbī remove even the most violent pitta.
Trapusa increases vāta and kapha while destroying pitta; kāliṅga and tucchaka increase vāta and kapha, whereas kaśeruka removes vāta and pitta.
Now follows the determination of the substances used for seasoning vegetables.
Śuṇṭhī, marica, and pippalī are considered to alleviate kapha and vāta;
hiṅgu destroys abdominal tumors, colic, and constipation, and removes vāta and kapha. (45)
Pacānī (yavānī),
dhānyaka, and jīva (bīja) remove vāta, pitta, and kapha.
Sauvarcala salt destroys constipation, and saindhava salt removes the three doṣas. // 47 //
But when these [herbs] are combined, cooked, fried, and made fragrant as a side dish,
or used as a drink and so forth, they dispel all the humors (doṣas), such as trembling and the like.
Thus ends the section on fruits and vegetables in the *Āyurvedamahodadhi* composed by Suṣeṇa.
(Ap 80) Now, the Śikhariṇī meter is described.
Half an *āḍhaka* of well-aged curd,
sixteen *palas* of sugar with the luster of the moon,
one *pala* of clarified butter, one *pala* of honey, and two *karṣas* of black pepper.
Half a pala of ginger and half a pala each of the four [aromatics] (the caturjātaka).
On a smooth cloth, this beautiful preparation, ground with the soft hands of a young woman and made fragrant with camphor powder,
was tasted by the Blessed One Madhusūdana— this delicious *rasālā* prepared by Vṛkodara. // 2 //
Thirty palas of curd, half a pala of agelā,
half a pala each of honey and clarified butter, and [half] a half-pala of black pepper.
Half of a *palā* (3).
One should dissolve eight *palas* of the powder into a pure cloth and strain it;
then, one should place this in a vessel scented with camphor and set it in the shade. // 4 //
This is called Śikhariṇī; it is radiant, increases strength, prolongs life, and indeed destroys all diseases. // 5 //
It destroys [diseases], and it is always beneficial for men suffering from thirst, pain, and obesity.
This is the second [variety], Śikhariṇī.
With *kapittha*, *mātuluṅga*, *elā*, *sārivā*, *ardhaka*, and *bījaka*,
well combined with sugar, ginger, sea salt, and powdered green gram;
One should always employ it as wholesome food; when the body is emaciated, it bestows nourishment.
Well-prepared curd and cream, having been placed [together] and bound in a cloth, should be squeezed thoroughly.
One should prepare a delightful mixture of various flowers and fruits in curd.
This excellent *śikhariṇī*, prepared with the finest curd-juice and ghee strained through a clean cloth, combined with salt in the proper measure, is like nectar. (9)
Rasālā destroys all the doṣas and subdues raktapitta;
another [variety] is śikhariṇī.
One should take a leaf of the *sanmātuliṅga* tree, along with *agelā*, *saraṅga*, and *pippalī*, combined with an equal amount of sugar.
And from *vyoṣa*, two *gadyāṇas* should be administered;
it should be bound in a white cloth and is equal to the [desired] vision.
Likewise, having subsequently ground together sugar, honey, and camphor with skill, this delicious *rasālā* was prepared as *śikhariṇī* by Suṣeṇadeva for the sake of his chariots and horses. (11)
When tasted by the Supreme Lord, Śikhariṇī destroys all fierce defects;
it also destroys all ailments arising from bile, blood, and phlegm, and it digests all kinds of food. (12)
The *Śikhariṇī* [verse] on the consumption of nectar.
One should take orange and pomegranate mixed with *madhuka* weighing one *pala*,
along with an equal portion of citron juice and grape juice, combined with jaggery and curd, and mixed with sugar and cumin.
The white variety is the best for drinks and as an aphrodisiac;
it is also excellent when applied to the feet as an aphrodisiac. Having mixed it with salt and *saindhava* salt, soak it all in this [liquid], then squeeze it out and prepare [the mixture].
For they are suitable for the king of mountains. // 13 //
Furthermore:
Sour citron, white cumin, black pepper, fresh ginger, and dry ginger, combined with camphor in appropriate proportions, are equal to curd that has stood overnight. (14)
The juice of all medicinal formulations, as well as that of the jujube fruit, mixed with ginger and combined with sugar, is like nectar to those who consume it. (15)
And well-ground fine cloth is a destroyer of blood-bile (raktapitta).
The Śikhariṇī [verse] named "Flowing with Moon-Amṛta."
Curds ground with sugar and combined with *mātuluṅga*, *kapittha*, *tittiḍīka*, and sour *dāḍima* fruits [should be applied] upon a clean cloth.
It is prepared with black pepper, cumin, the four spices (cāturjātaka), and fragrant grasses;
when eaten together with fresh ginger, it becomes a nectar-like *rasālā*.
Haritaki pacifies all diseases, eliminates burning sensations and pitta, removes excess blood, is wholesome, and facilitates the downward movement of all vata. (18)
This *śikhariṇī* has been described, composed by Suṣeṇa;
and furthermore:
This [preparation] is supreme when combined with curd, jaggery, cumin, ginger, and fresh ginger.
Well-prepared and ground with sugar, this *rasālā* is like nectar;
it pacifies all hardships and destroys all types of diarrhea. (Ap 83, 20)
Haritaki removes an excess of bile and destroys bilious diarrhea;
this Rasala, prepared by King Suṣeṇa, is indeed like nectar. (21)
Thus ends the section on *śikhariṇī* meters composed by Suṣeṇa.
Now follows the section on consonants.
Asafoetida, black pepper, cumin, and great medicinal herbs (mahauṣadha), powdered in increasing proportions by threefold increments,
along with bishop’s weed (dīpyaka) and suraṇa—
this is always desired for use with meat broths. (1)
Equal parts of barley and cumin, with twice that amount of *sūraṇa* root, combined with a small amount of salt, produce a fragrant condiment (*vyañjana*). // 2 //

This wholesome remedy removes all diseases and destroys wind-related disorders and hemorrhoids; it consists of ginger, black pepper, long pepper, and powdered *nāga* (mineral pitch) in equal parts. // 3 //
Wherever one drinks well-prepared buttermilk mixed with *cavya*, *citraka*, and the essence of *kāpittha*, along with rock salt (*saindhava*).

This indeed is the most excellent medicinal preparation, which wards off all types of wind disorders, pacifies even severe abdominal tumors (gulma), and was prepared by Suṣeṇa for the benefit of men. // 5 //
This is the supreme medicine for all wind-related diseases (vātāmaya) of men;
and furthermore:
Long pepper, bishop's weed, dry ginger, chaba pepper, and leadwort; // 6 //
Long pepper, long pepper root, coriander, cumin,
rock salt, black cumin, pomegranate, myrobalan, and emblic myrobalan possess a pleasing fragrance. (7)
Having cooked this mixture for a period equal to a Kalpa with buttermilk and a lump of ghee,
it removes Vata and Kapha, is pleasing to the heart, and is supremely effective in increasing the appetite.

It destroys diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātīsāra) and colic, cuts through wind-born abdominal tumors (vātagulma), and removes cough and asthma. It is formidable, excellent, and supreme for those with weak digestion;
it is declared to be always wholesome, and is remembered as the best of the hard varieties. // 10 //
A small cauldron (made of clay).
Long pepper, ginger,
long pepper root, cavya, black salt, rock salt, coriander, long pepper, rock salt, the essence of unripe wood-apple, pomegranate, and asafoetida.
The well-ripened *āmalaka* fruit from the hands of young women, properly processed.

Suṣeṇa, the king of physicians who knows all that is to be known, removes the primary wind disorder, phlegm, burning sensations, dysuria, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, and diarrhea caused by āmavāta.
She prepares a side dish of wood-apple that is kept secret from the king. // 12 //
// And furthermore //
The three pungents (trikaṭuka), ajamodā, rock salt (saindhava), the two types of cumin (jīraka), fresh butter-milk (karamathita), kapittha, citraka, and long pepper (pippalī)—
these should be combined there, having been made into a powder in equal proportions.
Boiled here with equal parts, it is combined with asafoetida. // 13 //
Salt, sugar, and grain, along with the essence of *mātuluṅga*,
should always be used as a condiment in disorders of phlegm and wind.
It also subdues wind, sluggish digestion, abdominal pain, and fainting that has persisted for a long time.
The Rasālā prepared by King Suṣeṇa is highly fragrant, disease-removing, and wholesome. // 14 //
Thus ends the section on consonants composed by the venerable Suṣeṇa.
Now the qualities of meat are being described.

Meat is the best among delicious foods; it provides excellent nourishment, is rich in fats, constantly maintains the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*), and is said to improve the complexion and promote corpulence.
When eaten, it provides satisfaction, fulfills desires, and removes disorders such as wind; therefore, one should always eat meat for the sake of pacifying bodily ailments. // 1 //
Now, the qualities of quail meat.

Lāva birds are sweet like snow, endowed with an astringent taste, aphrodisiac, digestive-stimulant, unctuous, and heart-pleasing; when cooked with pungent spices, they are astringent and beneficial in all types of combined humoral disorders (saṃnipāta). // 2 //
Lāvarū (bhā-)
Now, the qualities of the black partridge (kṛṣṇatittiri).
The white partridge is slightly heavy and warm, sweet, highly aphrodisiac, and promotes intelligence and digestive fire;
it is strengthening and cures disorders of phlegm-fever as well as diseases of wind (vāta) and others. // 3 //
Black partridge (commentary)
(Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 8.6) Now follows the Gauratittiri sacrifice.
The white partridge (*gaura-tittiri*) is digestive, removes phlegm, is dry, and greatly subdues bile;
it destroys phlegm and overcomes both blood and bile. Now, the *kāpiñjala* [partridge]:

The Kapiñjala bird is always recommended for those suffering from blood and bile disorders; it is extremely cooling, light, strengthening, highly aphrodisiac, a remover of mild skin diseases, a destroyer of worms, and a healer of urinary ailments. It generates semen and digestive fire in cases of emaciation caused by the loss of fat.
It quickly effects the dissolution of wind and blood disorders and is a destroyer of diseases caused by bile. // 4 //
Now, the qualities of the eggplant (vārtāka).
It is recommended for diseases arising from urinary disorders (prameha), skin eruptions (piḍikā), and worms, as well as for those dominated by Vāta.
It destroys tumors (kīla) born of Vāta, blood, Pitta, and Kapha, and it is light, curing abdominal tumors (gulma), weak digestion, and loss of appetite. (5)
Now, the qualities of the *krakara* and *upacakrika* [medicinal plants].
It is light, aphrodisiac, a nourisher of strength, pleasing to the heart, and likewise stimulates the appetite. (Sakrakaropacakrikā)
(Āyurveda-prakāśa 87) Now, the qualities of peacock meat.

Kāṣāya is pungent, highly aphrodisiac, and produces vitality; it is delicious, beneficial for the throat, alkaline, appetizing, and an antidote to poison. It destroys weak digestion, improves the voice, is purifying, generates great joy, and strengthens the sense of hearing.
Peacock meat is always unctuous and hot, and it pacifies wind, blood disorders, and bile.
Indeed, they desire peacock meat to be consumed during the winter, the cool season, and the spring.
Now, the qualities of chicken meat:
Hot, very sweet, strengthening the strength and voice, aphrodisiac, always nourishing, unctuous in its post-digestive effect, and a great subduer of *vāta*, it produces fat, *kapha*, and lethargy;
it promotes longevity in cases of wasting (*kṣaya*), and is recommended for irregular fever, urinary disorders (*meha*), and vomiting.
For the Kukkuṭaka has been declared to be the pacifier of the humors and the destroyer of all diseases. // 9 //
Now, the qualities of the pigeon and other such birds.
The pigeon, the dove, the *bhṛṅgarāja*, the jaṭī, the *kuliṅga*, the domestic bird, and the cuckoo;
the *bhedāśi*, the *ḍiṇḍī*, the parrot, the *sārikā*, the *vālūka*, and the wagtail—these green-colored birds are praised.

Fruits that are astringent, windy, and dry, when consumed as food by those living in arid regions, alleviate pitta and kapha; they are said to increase pitta, bind the urine, and diminish the feces. // 11 //
They always produce defects; they cause dissension, are impure and corrupting,
salty, cold, increase phlegm, act as aphrodisiacs, and are always difficult to digest.
They produce constipation and excessive urine; they are said to cause burning of the mouth and bile disorders.
They cause undigested matter (āma) and flatulence, generate the three doṣas, and produce delusion and a bad taste in the mouth.
They are difficult to digest, increase digestive fire and strength, remove fatigue, and cause foul odor and phlegm. (12)
These, when consumed daily during the rainy season, indeed destroy the multitude of humors;
they are all capable of moving through the air, strengthening, aphrodisiac, and very difficult to digest. (13)
The qualities of the kauliṅga bird.
The *kauliṅga* (fish) is sweet, highly aphrodisiac, increases *kapha*, and breaks up seminal stones;

it removes *pitta* and blood disorders, generates semen excessively, and produces moisture and sweetness in the mouth. It is strengthening, subdues *vāta*, destroys worms, and is beneficial for eye diseases.
It pacifies those with evil names, destroys the wind of particularity, and is always difficult to digest. // 14 //
The qualities of village-dwellers.
All domestic [meats] dispel wind, are nourishing, increase phlegm and bile, are sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect, stimulate digestion, and increase strength. // 15 //
The qualities of a pigeon.
The pigeon-colored sandalwood (*kāpota*) is heavy, very cooling, unctuous, slow-acting, and provocative of *śleṣman* (phlegm).
It is beneficial for *pitta* (bile) and, like old age, it wears away [the heat] from the *candana*.
It is the best for removing fatigue when semen is depleted, and it is excellent for difficult urination during the summer heat.
He becomes one who applies himself to delusion among men, acting with force for the sake of the body. // 16 //
Now,
the qualities of the meat of wild animals.
Jāṅgala meat destroys disorders of the bladder, is heavy, cures chronic rhinitis, is light in digestion, is not cold, and is neither excessively unctuous nor burning in nature. (17)
Now, the qualities of the flesh of goats and sheep.
Goat meat is neither too cold, nor heavy, nor unctuous, and it does not aggravate the *doṣas*.
Because its nature is similar to that of the bodily tissues (*dhātu*), it is non-obstructive and nourishing.
The flesh of the *saurabha* (wild ox) is nourishing, increases *pitta* and *kapha*, and is heavy. (18)
Now, the qualities of venison:

The meat of the ena deer is pleasing to the heart and strength-promoting; it subdues bile and blood disorders, and in cases of jaundice and emaciation accompanied by burning sensations, it quickly destroys diseases of phlegm and wind as well as tumors (kīla).
It cures splenic enlargement, abdominal distension, and constipation, is supreme in removing fever, and brings an end to obesity.
It should be employed when semen is diminished; it is appetizing, light, and cures asthma and cough. // 19 //

The fat derived from the tail is a remover of phlegm and wind, bestowing luster and nourishment; it may cause wind, blood disorders, and bile, yet it removes intoxication, destroys poison, and cuts through asthma and cough.
Now, the qualities of rabbit meat:

The meat of the hare is strengthening, increases vitality, is supreme in alleviating fever, is excellent for those with diminished semen, is commended for wind-related disorders, and destroys diseases of the skin. (20)
Now, the qualities of the meat of camels and other such animals.
Camel meat with salt, and the meat of animals with uncloven hooves— this group of meat from the arid (jāṅgala) regions is said to cause little obstruction of the channels.
The deer and birds that dwell in the vicinity of Dule’s waterfall, whose range extends to distant waters, are considered to be highly susceptible to excessive secretions.
Now, the virtues of forest-dwellers.
Due to their sweetness, heavy foods are superior for treating excessive dryness, burning sensations, emaciation, intoxication, and poisoning; they provide strength through urine and feces,
cure cough and hemorrhoids, constantly alleviate wind and bile disorders, and, when unctuous, remove leanness.
All those forest-dwelling animals alleviate *kapha* and are always beneficial for urinary disorders (*meha*). // 23 //
Now follows the consideration of the relative heaviness and lightness of meats.
River fish are not to be eaten when they are large, because they move between the tail and the mouth; however, among those born in lakes and ponds, the crane-fish (sārasa) is especially light.
Since their range is not far-reaching, they are therefore called *utsoda-pādalas*; though slightly released at the top of the head, they are exceedingly heavy. (25)
Below, the heavy syllables are to be known; the fish and the lotuses are traditionally taught.
Among them, the examination of the chest is first; the limb [of the meter] is traditionally taught as light.

The head, shoulders, waist, back, thighs, and the stomach—these one should know to be heavy in the order mentioned; however, wind (vāta) is lighter than the preceding, [and the others become progressively lighter]. (The latter ones are indeed lighter in succession. // 27 //
In the bodies of all living beings, the middle part is declared to be heavy;
for men, the upper part is heavy, while for women, it is the lower part. (Ap 91, 28)
The chest and neck of birds are especially considered heavy; however, the middle part of birds is said to be light when they are flying or fluttering. 29.
The flesh of leaf-eating birds is exceedingly dry,
whereas the flesh of carnivorous birds is highly nourishing.
Fish that feed on grain increase pitta and subdue vata;
likewise do those from arid lands, marshy regions, domestic animals, carnivores, and single-hoofed animals. (31)
The *prasahas*, those that dwell in holes, and those defined by their specific groups, as well as the peckers and the scratchers—these become lighter [to digest] in the order mentioned. (32)
Now, the qualities of boar meat:
Boar meat always cures the disorders of wind (vāta) and dyspepsia (durnāma),

destroys worms, is unctuous, promotes perspiration, is aphrodisiac, cooling, and bestows strength; it increases heart disease, relieves cough and asthma, pacifies urinary disorders (prameha), and destroys hiccup and wind.
Pork meat, however, is beneficial for the eyes, causes a burning sensation, and always removes vertigo. (33)
Now, the qualities of conch, tortoise, and so forth.
Conch, tortoise, and others have a sweet taste and post-digestive effect; they provide wind, are unctuous, cold, beneficial for pitta, and increase feces and phlegm. (34)
The black crab among them is strengthening,
heating, and dispels wind; the white one promotes healing, increases excrement and urine, and subdues wind and bile.
Now, the qualities of fish.
Fish from rivers are sweet, heavy, and alleviate sluggishness and heat;
they increase blood and bile, are warm, aphrodisiac, unctuous, and cause scanty stools. (36)
Among them, the *kaṣāyānurasas* is the best; its disciple is the *śaivālabhojana*; and the *rohita* removes wind (*māruta*) and does not excessively aggravate bile (*pitta*). // 37 //
Fish are of two kinds; those born from water and those born from the earth (?).
Therefore, the former should be conceived as being of five types.
There may be [waters] from rivers, from wells, from lakes, arising from lightning, from tanks, and likewise from the ocean. // 38 //
Now, the suitability of specific fish according to the divisions of the seasons.
Fish born in mountain streams during the spring season are beneficial,
whereas those found in the summer season should be avoided.
All those born in ponds during the rainy season produce humors that are both unctuous and powerful. (39)
In the autumn season, fish born in mountain torrents and those from wells are beneficial; in the winter, those born in the ocean are so.
In the cold season, the fish are cranes; in spring, they are those born in ponds;
in summer, the fish are those from hot springs; and in the rainy season, they are those born in tanks.
In autumn, fish from mountain torrents [are best]; in winter, those originating from wells;
a whirlpool in a stream from the six families is considered the lightest to catch.
Now, according to their habitat, the qualities of fish are described.
Those produced from lakes and ponds are known to be unctuous and of sweet taste. // 41 //
Fish from ponds (kauṣya) are aphrodisiac, increase wind, and cause phlegm; they produce abdominal tumors (gulma), prostate enlargement (aṣṭhīlā), constipation (ānāha), and skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
Fish from tanks (tāḍāga) are heavy, nourishing, cold, aphrodisiac, and cause excessive urination.
Those born in mountain torrents (nirjhara) are as [heavy] as those from tanks, yet they are purifying (medhya).
And they bestow stable longevity and strength. // 43 //
My tears [are like] great lakes;
those with little water are considered strong.
Sea water is heavy, hot, dry, sweet, increases phlegm (*śleṣman*), and subdues wind (*vāta*)—it is high in phlegm and subdues wind.

It increases unctuousness, provides strength, causes constipation and flatulence, is prescribed for conditions of excessive pitta and deficient kapha, and is always wholesome and highly pleasing to the heart.
And it would produce constipation and the affliction of cold winds if consumed in excess. (44)
The Rohita fish from the sea pacifies the three doṣas, is beneficial for the heart, destroys pitta, removes vāta, is recommended in all diseases, and stimulates the digestive fire.
Sea fish are heavy, unctuous, sweet, and not excessively heating;
they alleviate Vāta, are aphrodisiac, increase fecal matter, and augment Kapha. (46)
Sea-born [fish] are especially strength-bestowing because they are meat-eaters; river-born fish are superior in quality to sea-born ones because of their lightness. // 47 //

Because they are even less salty than that, the well-water and the pond-water possess superior qualities; and because of its richness and its sweet flavor, the pond-water possesses qualities even greater than the well-water.
Now, the qualities of the *krakara* and other [birds].
The *krakara* bird destroys constipation, flatulence, and urinary disorders; it removes phlegm and wind.
It alleviates fat, phlegm, and wind, and cures hiccups and ailments of flatulence. (49)
The Rohita fish is excellent; it destroys bile, removes wind, is nourishing, pacifies wind, subdues wind, stimulates the digestive fire, and is light.
Among all fish, it is the heaviest, yet it is the best, stimulating the digestive fire and destroying wind.
It provides relish, promotes semen, and destroys the disorder of urinary calculi. // 51 //
The Guru-fish.

Śṛṅgī is considered to destroy wind (vāta), stimulate the appetite, act as an aphrodisiac, and subdue phlegm (kapha); it is clear, virilific, increases digestive fire, and is esteemed for both wind and phlegm disorders.
Pāṭhīna provides strength, acts as an aphrodisiac, generates semen, and constantly produces phlegm.
Therefore, the rohītaka is beneficial, strength-promoting, increases wind (vāta), and increases phlegm (śleṣman). // 52 //
Thus say the followers of the Matsya Purāṇa.
Thus ends the section on meats in the *Āyurvedamahodadhi* composed by Suṣeṇa.
Now, the procedures and benefits of physical exercise, dry massage, and oil massage are described.
The massage of kings should always be performed by wrestlers skilled in the art of rubbing, using *śrīnārāyaṇa* oil, *campaka* oil, *japā* oil, or other oils,
along with the four products of the cow (*cāturjātaka*), cloves, saffron, turmeric, nut-grass, and spikenard.
One should perform an unguent with a powder consisting of fried masūra and mung beans. // 1 //
One should massage [the area] after anointing it with oil prepared from wind-alleviating herbs;
one should not perform a dry massage, for that indeed provokes the wind (vāta). // 2 //
Having attained sleep through ease, with his senses and self perfectly serene, maintaining a very light digestive function, he partakes of food in moderation.
Exhausted by the weight of fatigue, with his limbs softened by oil, the lord of the earth should approach the master of the bathhouse for a massage. // 3 //
Anointing the body with oil removes fatigue and wind, bestows strength, and brings firmness to the physique.

Rubbing the body with medicinal powders (*udvartana*) produces luster for the limbs and conquers fat, phlegm, and lethargy. It promotes longevity, clarifies the heart, and eliminates itching, exhaustion, and vomiting from the body.
By bathing alone with these waters, whether cold or warm, according to the season, this [benefit] is obtained.
Now, the qualities of physical exercise.
It bestows capacity for all activities, lightness in the limbs, supreme radiance, sharpness of the senses,
the reduction of fat, enthusiasm of the mind, firmness of the body, and by its power, the pacification of calamities.
In the winter season, one should practice exertion, having been accustomed to cold during the springtime.
Now, regarding those two [types of persons] who are exempt from physical exertion:

Those afflicted with wind-disorders or accompanied by bile-diseases, the very young, the very old, the emaciated, those who have over-eaten, those with weak digestion, and those who avoid unctuous liquids and foods—these should be avoided during the improper times for treatment. // 6 //
Just as there is no proper cooking in a pot that is neither uncovered nor properly closed,
O kings, so too for one who has not obtained sleep and lacks physical exercise, there is no proper digestion.
(Ap 96) Now, the benefits of massaging the feet.
It removes wind-related diseases, pacifies phlegm, brings about luster and clarity, destroys discoloration of the skin, promotes appetite, bestows firmness upon all the limbs,
kindles the digestive fire, generates strength, and eliminates excessive perspiration and fat.
The sages always prescribe the trampling with the feet as the best [remedy] for living beings. // 8 //
Now, those [actions] excluding the massaging of the feet.
For one who is delicate, has weak digestion, whose strength is somewhat diminished,
or who is of bilious temperament, foot-massage should never be performed.
Diseases do not approach one whose limbs have been perspired through exercise and massaged with the feet, just as serpents do not approach Garuda.
That which is performed by the best of wrestlers as a massage makes the body golden-hued and immediately bestows firmness upon the limbs; it extends lightness in all activities. (11)
He conquers wind-disease and brings about [health]...
O Lord of All, this is my vow; for him, that very same commitment is like food for one who is hungry. 12.
He who, out of a state of delusion and greed, would eat food that is like sleeping vipers, venomous serpents, or fires—such a person is one who would awaken them in a contrary manner. (13)
He who desires the female of the *kokavanya* bird should eat at night;
and he who is a lover by day should [eat] these at night like a *cakora*. (14)
(Ap 97) Now, the rules regarding eating.
Due to the disappearance of the fierce sun, the lotuses of the heart and the navel contract;
therefore, those who are the best among the knowers of medical science should not eat at night. 15.
One should not perform the worship of the gods, eat, or sleep in the open air;
nor should one do so in darkness, during the twilight hours, or in a dwelling without a roof.
He who is distressed by the constraints of eating, tasting, and voiding excrement—
due to the disappearance of fearlessness, his pride is as base as that of a crow.
One should not eat food that is discolored, putrid, decomposed, foul-smelling, or tasteless; nor should one consume food that is overcooked or unwholesome, as these are prohibited.
Having eaten, one should avoid [certain things].
One who desires their own welfare should never consume curd, pigeon-colored milk-rice, vehicles, draft animals, or much milk, nor water from a pond, immediately after a meal. 19.
The procedure for eating.
One should eat food that is wholesome, moderate in quantity, well-cooked, pleasing to the eyes and nose, and thoroughly examined; neither too hastily nor too slowly.
Excessive eating, eating at the wrong time, eating too little, and irregular eating must be abandoned.
One should perform that which pacifies what has been spoken of, which is beneficial for strength and life, in due order. // 21 //
The sequence of eating.

At the beginning, one should eat what is sweet and unctuous; in the middle, what is salty and sour; and at the end, what is dry and liquid. After having eaten, one should never consume anything whatsoever.
And the fourfold nature of fire.
The digestive fire (*vahni*) of men is of four types: sweet (*madhu*), bitter (*tikta*), irregular (*viṣama*), and even (*sama*).
When the fire is weak (*manda*), food is light; when it is sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), food is heavy and bitter (*tikta*).
Because of you, one might eat poison as if it were wholesome, and even what is wholesome as if it were poison.
Now begins the section on the enumeration of foods.
Food eaten at a single time according to one's desire is digested easily; however, one who possesses a balanced digestive fire may eat twice a day in moderate measure. (24)
Whatever is hard to digest, difficult to break down, or causes a burning sensation—all that should be avoided at night; one should instead practice [eating] what is liquid and light. (25)
Now follows the examination of food defiled by poison.
Here, the crow utters various notes, and the young peacock,
the offspring of the crested one, becomes joyful and brownish-hued.
The curlew rejoices and the cock crows; the parrot vomits and the monkey burns.
The eyes of the cakora bird turn red and white from the sight of poison;
the gait of the swan falters, and flies settle upon it. (27)
Just as fire crackles and bursts forth intensely upon contact with salt, so too is the contamination of food by poison clearly perceived. (28)
May Suṣeṇa, for my benefit, quickly grant me life and favor for my son.
Thus ends the chapter on the rules for eating in the Great Ocean of Āyurveda composed by Suṣeṇa.
Now, the qualities of betel are described.
